facts.text: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
Botanically, bananas are berries — but strawberries are not.
A day on Venus is longer than its year: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to turn once, but only about 225 to orbit the Sun.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings.
Sharks are older than trees: the first sharks appeared about 450 million years ago, the first trees roughly 385 million years ago.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
Babies are born with about 270 bones; many of them fuse as they grow, so adults have about 206.
The shortest war on record, the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896, lasted less than an hour.
Butterflies taste with their feet — they have taste receptors on them.
The University of Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire: teaching there began around 1096, while Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres every year.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
At its triple point, water can boil and freeze at the same time.
Contrary to a popular myth, the Great Wall of China cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.
Koalas have fingerprints that are remarkably similar to human ones.
Venus is the hottest planet in the Solar System, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
The word “robot” comes from the Czech word “robota”, meaning forced labour. It was introduced in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.
In 1947, engineers found a real moth stuck in the Harvard Mark II computer and taped it into their logbook as the “first actual case of bug being found”.
There are roughly three trillion trees on Earth — more than the number of stars in the Milky Way.
The summit of Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre — not Mount Everest.
Russia spans eleven time zones.
A lightning bolt can heat the air to around 30,000 °C — about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Crows can recognise individual human faces and remember them for years.
The dot over the letters i and j is called a tittle.
A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
Honey barely spoils: archaeologists have found honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that was still preserved after thousands of years.
Sea otters often hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart.
The Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 centimetres taller in summer, because the iron expands in the heat.
There are more possible games of chess than atoms in the observable universe.

stories: Once upon a time, a small lighthouse stood on a rock where no ships ever came. Every night it shone anyway, patient and bright. One stormy evening, a lost fishing boat saw the light, turned toward it, and made it safely home. The lighthouse never knew it — but it had been waiting its whole life for exactly that night.

A robot who could only count decided to learn about the world. It counted raindrops, stars and the words in every book it could find. One day a child asked it: “What's the most important number?” The robot thought for a long time and said: “One — the person I'm talking to.”

There was once a snail who wanted to see the ocean. Everyone laughed: “It's a hundred miles away!” The snail just kept going, one slimy inch at a time. Years later, a seagull spotted a very old, very happy snail sitting on the beach, watching the waves.

A girl planted a seed and watered it every day, but nothing happened. After a month her brother said, “Give up, it's dead.” She kept watering. In the spring, the whole garden was green — the seed had been a bamboo, spending all that time growing roots before it ever showed a leaf.

{Topic}, you quiet wonder of the day,
you find a way to brighten every grey;
in every thought, in every word I write,
you are a spark that keeps the world in light.

I asked the wind to tell me about {topic},
it whispered softly through the trees;
some things are best not said, but felt —
like {topic}, carried on the breeze.

Of all the things I've read and known,
of all the words I've learned to weigh,
there's something about {topic}
that makes me want to stay.

Morning comes, and {topic} is there,
as steady as the rising sun;
it asks for nothing, gives its share,
and stays when all the day is done.

howto.title: Nudeln kochen
steps: Viel Wasser (etwa 1 Liter pro 100 g) zum Kochen bringen und gut salzen.
Die meisten getrockneten Nudeln brauchen 8–12 Minuten – die Packungsangabe ist ein guter Richtwert.
Eine Minute vor Ende probieren: weich, aber noch mit etwas Biss (al dente).
Vor dem Abgießen eine Tasse Nudelwasser aufheben – damit hält die Soße besser.

howto.title: Reis kochen
steps: Reis waschen, bis das Wasser fast klar ist.
Etwa 1,5 Tassen Wasser pro Tasse weißem Reis (Vollkorn: 2).
Aufkochen, Deckel drauf, Hitze klein: 12–15 Minuten (Vollkorn 35–40).
5–10 Minuten zugedeckt ruhen lassen, dann mit einer Gabel auflockern.

howto.title: Eier kochen
steps: Das Ei vorsichtig mit einem Löffel ins kochende Wasser legen.
Weich: 6 Minuten · mittel: 8 Minuten · hart: 10–11 Minuten.
Danach kurz in kaltes Wasser – dann lässt es sich viel leichter schälen.

howto.title: Einfache Pfannkuchen
steps: 200 g Mehl, 2 TL Backpulver, eine Prise Salz und 1 EL Zucker mischen.
1 Ei, 300 ml Milch und 2 EL geschmolzene Butter unterrühren, bis der Teig glatt ist.
Kleine Kellen in einer leicht gebutterten Pfanne bei mittlerer Hitze backen.
Wenden, wenn oben Bläschen entstehen – etwa 1–2 Minuten pro Seite.

howto.title: Was bei Halsschmerzen hilft
steps: Warme Getränke – Tee mit Honig und Zitrone ist ein Klassiker.
Mehrmals täglich mit warmem Salzwasser gurgeln (ein halber Teelöffel Salz auf ein Glas).
Lutschtabletten und genug Schlaf; Rauch und sehr trockene Luft meiden.
Zum Arzt, wenn es länger als eine Woche dauert, hohes Fieber dazukommt oder Schlucken bzw. Atmen schwerfällt.

howto.title: Was bei Kopfschmerzen hilft
steps: Ein großes Glas Wasser trinken – leichter Flüssigkeitsmangel ist eine häufige Ursache.
Eine Weile ruhig und abgedunkelt ausruhen, weg vom Bildschirm.
Ein kühles Tuch auf der Stirn oder ein kurzer Spaziergang an der frischen Luft.
Bei sehr starken, plötzlichen oder immer wiederkehrenden Kopfschmerzen zum Arzt.

howto.title: Gut durch eine Erkältung
steps: So viel wie möglich ausruhen und viel trinken.
Warme Suppe, Tee mit Honig und Dampf (heiße Dusche) lindern das verstopfte Gefühl.
Meerwasser-Nasenspray hilft bei verstopfter Nase.
Die meisten Erkältungen sind nach 7–10 Tagen vorbei – bei hohem Fieber oder längerer Dauer zum Arzt.

howto.title: Was beim Schlafen hilft
steps: Die letzte halbe Stunde keine Bildschirme – lieber etwas auf Papier lesen.
Ab dem frühen Nachmittag keinen Kaffee mehr.
Jeden Tag zur gleichen Zeit ins Bett und aufstehen, auch am Wochenende.
Wenn du nach 20 Minuten nicht schläfst: aufstehen und etwas Ruhiges machen.

hike_tips:
Ein paar Wander-Basics:

• Lieber eine etwas kürzere Route wählen und morgens das Wetter checken
• Früh losgehen – kühler und weniger voll
• Jemandem sagen, wo du unterwegs bist
• Keine brandneuen Schuhe, vorher einlaufen
• Umdrehen, wenn das Wetter umschlägt – der Berg läuft nicht weg
hike_bring:
Für eine Tageswanderung:

• Genug Wasser und Snacks (Nüsse, Brot, Obst)
• Zwiebellook: warme Schicht und Regenjacke, auch bei Sonne
• Feste Schuhe mit gutem Profil
• Sonnencreme, Sonnenbrille, Kappe
• Handy mit Offline-Karte und Powerbank
• Ein kleines Erste-Hilfe-Set und Pflaster
hike_water: Ungefähr einen halben Liter pro Stunde, bei Hitze oder steilen Strecken mehr. Für vier Stunden sind zwei Liter ein guter Start.

cost.cheap: {x} ist im Vergleich zu Westeuropa eher günstig – Essen gehen, Nahverkehr und Museen sind bezahlbar.
cost.mid: {x} liegt im Mittelfeld: nicht billig, aber machbar. Hotels im Zentrum und Touristenlokale gehen ins Geld, lokale Restaurants und der Nahverkehr halten es im Rahmen.
cost.pricey: {x} ist eher teuer, vor allem Hotels und Essen gehen. Früh buchen, etwas außerhalb wohnen und dort essen, wo Einheimische essen, hilft viel.

apologize:
Eine gute Entschuldigung ist einfach:

• Sag konkret, was dir leidtut
• Kein „aber“ – nicht rausreden
• Zeig, dass du verstehst, wie es sich für sie angefühlt hat
• Sag, was du anders machen willst

Und dann hör ihr richtig zu.

lonely_ideas:
Ein paar Ideen:

• Ein, zwei Tage pro Woche im Café oder Co-Working arbeiten
• Etwas Regelmäßiges: Sportverein, Kurs, Chor, Lauftreff
• Ehrenamt – man lernt Leute kennen und tut Gutes
• Heute einer alten Freundin oder einem alten Freund schreiben

Klingt etwas davon nach dir?
ideas_liked: Schön, dass dir was davon gefällt! Schon einer davon ist ein toller Anfang.

work_stress: Das klingt nach richtig viel. Was belastet dich gerade am meisten – die Menge oder der Druck?

work_tips:
Ein paar Dinge, die oft helfen:

• Aufschreiben, was ansteht, und die drei wichtigsten Punkte markieren
• Mit dem Chef offen über Prioritäten sprechen: „Was soll zuerst fertig werden?“
• Kleine Pausen einplanen – auch fünf Minuten an der frischen Luft
• Nach Feierabend bewusst abschalten, Handy weg

Wenn es dauerhaft zu viel ist, ist das kein persönliches Versagen.

joke_explain: Ha, berechtigt – das ist ein Wortspiel, und Wortwitze sind Geschmackssache. 😄 Soll ich einen anderen versuchen?
Der lebt von der Doppeldeutigkeit – zugegeben, nicht mein bester. Noch einer?
g63.vs_chatgpt: Kein neuronales Netz hier – ich bestehe aus Zählen, Regeln und einem genauen Gedächtnis. Der Vorteil: offline, klein, durchschaubar, jede Tatsache mit Quelle. Der Nachteil: Ich bin weniger flexibel als ChatGPT und sage öfter „weiß ich nicht“.
quit: Kündigen ist ein großer Schritt. Willst du eher etwas Neues – oder weg von etwas?
Oh, das klingt ernst. Was ist der Hauptgrund?
quit_money: Das ist der schwierige Teil – Geld ist ein echter Grund. Könntest du dich schon umsehen, während du noch dort bist? Dann wählst du, statt zu flüchten.
Verständlich. Ohne etwas Neues zu kündigen ist riskant. Vielleicht jetzt schon still bewerben, damit die Geldsorge nicht für dich entscheidet?
quit_view: Ich würde nicht kündigen, bevor etwas Neues in Aussicht ist. Ich würde mich jetzt umsehen, aufschreiben, was der Chef macht, und notfalls mit der Personalabteilung reden. Auf eigene Faust zu gehen fühlt sich viel besser an.
Ehrlich? Ich würde mich leise woanders bewerben und mir eine Frist setzen, etwa drei Monate. Ändert sich nichts, hast du dann Optionen statt nur einen schlechten Chef.
g63.say_no:
Ein paar Wege, höflich Nein zu sagen:

• „Ich würde gern helfen, aber ich bin mit X und Y ausgelastet. Was davon soll ich dafür liegen lassen?“
• „Diese Woche schaffe ich das nicht – geht es auch bis Montag?“
• „Ich bin dafür nicht die Beste/der Beste, aber frag doch mal [Name].“

Der Trick: freundlich bleiben, kurz begründen, eine Alternative anbieten – keine lange Entschuldigung nötig.
sleep: Nie! Träume habe ich leider auch keine. Und du – schläfst du genug?
Schlafen kenne ich nicht – ich bin da, sobald du die App öffnest. Schläfst du gut?
lucky: Vielleicht! Aber einmal ausschlafen am Sonntag würde ich schon gern ausprobieren.
Kommt drauf an – du hast dafür Träume und Nickerchen. Klingt nach einem fairen Tausch.
weird: Komisch im guten Sinn, hoffe ich! 😄

g65.friends_tips:
Freunde finden als Erwachsener:

• Geh dorthin, wo regelmäßig dieselben Leute sind: ein Kurs, ein Verein, ein Sportteam, ein Ehrenamt.
• Wiederholung zählt mehr als der erste Eindruck – bleib ein paar Wochen dabei.
• Schlag selbst etwas Kleines vor: einen Kaffee nach dem Kurs.
• Sag Ja zu Einladungen, auch wenn du müde bist.

Es dauert ein paar Monate – das ist normal.
shy: Das ist völlig okay – viele sind schüchtern. Am leichtesten geht es bei einer gemeinsamen Aktivität, etwa einem Kurs oder Verein: Man redet über die Sache, nicht über sich, und dieselben Gesichter jede Woche erledigen den Rest.
Schüchtern zu sein verhindert keine Freundschaften – es geht nur langsamer und stetiger besser. Ein wöchentlicher Kurs ist ideal: kein großer erster Eindruck nötig.
new_city: Ein Neuanfang in einer fremden Stadt ist hart, gerade am Anfang. Wohin bist du gezogen?
Das kenne ich von vielen – die ersten Monate in einer neuen Stadt können einsam sein. Was hat dich dorthin gebracht?
close: Jemanden zu verlieren, dem man so nahestand, hinterlässt eine große Lücke. Wie war {p} so?
Das macht es noch schwerer. Klingt, als hätte {p} dir sehr viel bedeutet. Woran erinnerst du dich am liebsten?
memory: Was für eine schöne Erinnerung. Jedes Mal, wenn du das machst, ist ein Stück von {d} dabei. Machst du das noch manchmal?
Danke, dass du das erzählst. Solche gemeinsamen Momente bleiben – sie gehören dir für immer.
miss: Natürlich vermisst du {d}. Das zeigt, wie viel {p} dir bedeutet hat.
Das ist ganz normal und zeigt, wie nah ihr euch wart. Gibt es etwas, das dich besonders an {d} erinnert?
impostor: Das Gefühl ist unglaublich verbreitet – es hat sogar einen Namen: Hochstapler-Syndrom. Du siehst die Highlights der anderen und deine eigenen Zweifel. Gut möglich, dass manche genau so über dich denken.
Man vergleicht leicht sein Inneres mit dem Äußeren der anderen. Die wurden für ihr Können eingestellt – und du auch. Was kannst du in deinem Job richtig gut?
g65.check_in: Das klingt wirklich schwer, und ich bin froh, dass du es mir erzählst. Darf ich fragen: Hast du Gedanken, dir etwas anzutun oder nicht mehr da sein zu wollen? Dann sprich bitte jetzt mit einem Menschen – die TelefonSeelsorge ist rund um die Uhr kostenlos erreichbar: 0800 111 0 111 oder 0800 111 0 222 (Österreich 142, Schweiz 143), im Notfall 112. Wenn nicht, bin ich trotzdem da – was war in letzter Zeit am schwersten?
nobody: Das klingt sehr einsam. Danke, dass du es mir sagst. Was ist passiert, dass du dich so fühlst?
Das ist ein schweres Gefühl. Ich bin da und höre zu – magst du erzählen, was los ist?
not_even: Das tut mir wirklich leid. Zu fühlen, dass nicht mal die eigene Familie sich kümmert, tut sehr weh. Du bist wichtig – und ich bin froh, dass du mit mir sprichst. Gibt es jemanden, dem du dich ein bisschen näher fühlst?
Das ist ein einsamer Ort, und es ist verständlich, dass es wehtut. Ist mit ihnen in letzter Zeit etwas passiert?
panic: Das tut mir leid – Panikattacken sind wirklich beängstigend. Geht es dir jetzt etwas besser?
Oh nein, das klingt furchtbar. Panikattacken fühlen sich an, als würde etwas Schlimmes passieren. Wie geht es dir gerade?
panic_bad: Das glaube ich dir. Der Körper schlägt Alarm, obwohl keine echte Gefahr da ist. Du hast es aber überstanden – es ist vorbeigegangen.
Natürlich – das Herzrasen und die Angst fühlen sich so echt an. Gut, dass du darüber sprichst.
g65.panic_tips:
Wenn es wieder passiert:

• Sag dir: Das ist eine Panikattacke, sie fühlt sich schlimm an, geht aber vorbei – meist nach 10–20 Minuten.
• Atme langsam aus – länger aus als ein (4 ein, 6–8 aus).
• Erde dich: Nenne 5 Dinge, die du siehst, 4, die du fühlst, 3, die du hörst.
• Danach: sei sanft zu dir.

Wenn Panikattacken öfter kommen, können Hausarzt oder Therapie wirklich helfen – sie sind gut behandelbar.
presentation: Präsentationen machen fast alle nervös – du bist in guter Gesellschaft. Hast du sie schon einmal laut geübt?
Ach, eine Präsentation – das kennt jeder. Wie gut fühlst du dich vorbereitet?
mess_up: Dann machst du eine kurze Pause, atmest durch und machst weiter – das Publikum merkt es meist gar nicht. In Erinnerung bleibt die Botschaft, nicht der Versprecher.
Ehrlich: Ein kleiner Fehler ist viel weniger schlimm, als es sich jetzt anfühlt. Die meisten Zuhörer sind auf deiner Seite. Lern die ersten zwei Sätze auswendig – der Rest kommt.
breakup: Das tut mir leid. Trennungen sind schwer, auch wenn sie richtig sind. Wie geht es dir?
Oh, das ist hart. Magst du erzählen, wie es dazu kam?
my_choice: Das ist ganz normal. Etwas zu beenden, weil es richtig ist, heißt nicht, dass es nicht wehtut – du verlierst etwas, das dir wichtig war. Sei gut zu dir.
Die schwere Entscheidung zu treffen braucht Mut, und es darf trotzdem wehtun. Beides stimmt. Wie kümmerst du dich gerade um dich?
friends: Das kann klappen, aber meist nicht sofort. Die meisten brauchen erst Abstand – ein paar Wochen oder Monate –, bis sich die Gefühle gelegt haben. Frag dich: Hilft dir die Freundschaft beim Heilen, oder hält sie die Wunde offen?
Vielleicht später. Direkt nach einer Trennung heißt 'Freunde bleiben' oft, dass einer auf mehr hofft. Gib euch Zeit.

sonst: Alles ruhig bei mir – ich bin da und plaudere gern. Und bei dir, was gibt's Neues?
Bei mir ist alles beim Alten. Und du – was läuft so bei dir?

essen: Weil sie für alle passt – dünn oder dick, schlicht oder schick, und kaum jemand sagt Nein zu einem Stück.
farbe: Sie wirkt ruhig und weit – Himmel, Meer, und irgendwie passt sie zu allem.
film: Zeitreisen, ein DeLorean und ein toller Soundtrack – was will man mehr? Und die Handlung greift wie ein Puzzle ineinander.
buch: Es ist kurz, freundlich und weise – „Man sieht nur mit dem Herzen gut“ bleibt einfach hängen.
musik: Sie haben sich in so wenigen Jahren so verändert – von einfachen Liebesliedern bis Abbey Road in nicht mal zehn Jahren.
tier: Drei Herzen, blaues Blut, und sie können Gläser öffnen und blitzschnell die Farbe wechseln – wie Außerirdische, nur echt.
jahreszeit: Nicht zu heiß, nicht zu kalt, und alles wird golden und rot. Gemütliche Zeit!
getränk: Weil es so viele Rituale darum gibt – die erste Tasse am Morgen, Espresso in Italien, Kaffeeklatsch mit Freunden.
sport: Kein Glück, nur Vorausdenken – und es gibt mehr mögliche Partien als Atome im Universum.
stadt: Hügel, gelbe Straßenbahnen, der Atlantik und Pastéis de Nata – alle, die darüber schreiben, klingen ein bisschen verliebt.
serie: Wie ein Chemielehrer Schritt für Schritt zu Heisenberg wird – darüber wird Jahre später noch gestritten.

Auch gut, danke der Nachfrage! Was steht bei dir heute an?

Puh, das ist viel. Ständig Extra-Aufgaben zermürben schnell. Weiß dein Chef, wie voll dein Teller schon ist?
chef_rat:
Was oft hilft:

• Schreib kurz alles auf, was gerade auf deinem Tisch liegt, mit grober Zeitschätzung.
• Geh damit zu deinem Chef und frag: „Was davon ist am wichtigsten? Wenn ich die neue Aufgabe übernehme, was kann warten?“
• So wird die Überlastung sichtbar, ohne nach Beschwerde zu klingen – und die Prioritäten entscheidet er, nicht dein Stress.

Ein paar Dinge, die eine Reise nach {X} leichter machen:

• Ausweis bzw. Reisepass rechtzeitig prüfen.
• Offline-Karten und eine Übersetzungs-App vorher herunterladen.

Was interessiert dich – Essen, Sehenswürdigkeiten oder Ausgehen?

rom: Essen in Rom: Carbonara, Cacio e Pepe und Amatriciana in einer Trattoria, Pizza al taglio auf die Hand, Supplì (frittierte Reisbällchen) und natürlich Gelato. Kaffee an der Theke ist günstiger als am Tisch.
paris: Essen in Paris: morgens ein Croissant aus der Boulangerie, mittags ein Croque Monsieur oder Steak Frites im Bistro, Crêpes vom Stand und Macarons aus der Pâtisserie. Das Mittagsmenü ist viel günstiger als abends.
london: Essen in London: Fish and Chips, ein Full English Breakfast, Sunday Roast im Pub und Curry in der Brick Lane. Auf dem Borough Market kann man von allem probieren.
barcelona: Essen in Barcelona: Tapas wie Patatas Bravas und Croquetas, Pan con Tomate, Paella am Meer und Churros mit Schokolade. Abendessen um 21 Uhr ist normal.
lissabon: Essen in Lissabon: Pastéis de Nata, gegrillte Sardinen, Bacalhau und eine Bifana. Probier auch einen Ginjinha, den Kirschlikör.
wien: Essen in Wien: Wiener Schnitzel, Sachertorte im Kaffeehaus, Apfelstrudel und spätabends eine Wurst vom Würstelstand.
amsterdam: Essen in Amsterdam: frische Stroopwafels vom Markt, Bitterballen zum Bier, Matjes für Mutige und holländische Pfannkuchen.
tokio: Essen in Tokio: Sushi an der Theke, Ramen, Yakitori unter den Bahngleisen und Onigiri aus dem Konbini – überraschend gut. Trinkgeld ist nicht üblich.
berlin: Essen in Berlin: Currywurst, Döner, ein großes Frühstück am Wochenende und sehr gutes vietnamesisches Essen.
sonst: Mein bester Essens-Tipp für {X}: iss dort, wo die Einheimischen essen – kleine Lokale eine Straße abseits der Sehenswürdigkeiten, Märkte und Mittagsmenüs.

name: Ich bin ENGRAMM!
ENGRAMM – schön, dass du fragst!

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele planeten (?:hat|gibt es in) (?:unser(?:em)? |das )?sonnensystem|wie viele planeten gibt es
fakten.a: Acht: Merkur, Venus, Erde, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus und Neptun. Pluto gilt seit 2006 als Zwergplanet.

fakten.q: (?:und )?(?:welcher planet ist|was ist) der rote planet|welcher planet wird (?:auch )?(?:der )?rote planet genannt|warum ist der mars rot
fakten.a: Der Mars ist der Rote Planet – seine Oberfläche ist mit eisenhaltigem Staub bedeckt, der quasi verrostet ist. Daher die rötliche Farbe.

fakten.q: (?:und )?(?:was|welches) ist das größte (?:säugetier|tier)(?: der welt| der erde)?
fakten.a: Der Blauwal – er wird bis zu 30 Meter lang und rund 150 Tonnen schwer. Er ist das größte Tier, das je gelebt hat.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele kontinente gibt es(?: auf der erde)?
fakten.a: Meist zählt man sieben: Afrika, Antarktika, Asien, Australien (Ozeanien), Europa, Nordamerika und Südamerika. In manchen Ländern werden Amerika oder Europa und Asien zusammengezählt.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer (?:war|ist) (?:der )?erste mensch auf dem mond|wer (?:war|ist) als erster auf dem mond|wer hat als erster den mond betreten
fakten.a: Neil Armstrong – er betrat am 20. Juli 1969 mit Apollo 11 als Erster den Mond. Buzz Aldrin folgte ihm etwa 20 Minuten später.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele beine hat (?:eine )?spinne|wie viele beine haben spinnen
fakten.a: Spinnen haben acht Beine – deshalb zählen sie nicht zu den Insekten (die haben sechs).

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer hat (?:das buch |den roman )?1984 geschrieben|wer ist der autor von 1984
fakten.a: George Orwell hat „1984“ geschrieben, erschienen 1949.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele (?:länder|staaten|mitglieder|mitgliedsstaaten) (?:hat die eu|sind in der eu|gibt es in der eu)
fakten.a: Die EU hat 27 Mitgliedsstaaten (seit dem Austritt Großbritanniens 2020).

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer hat die glühbirne erfunden
fakten.a: Viele haben daran getüftelt – aber Thomas Edisons Kohlefaden-Glühbirne von 1879 war die erste praktische, langlebige; Joseph Swan baute fast zeitgleich eine ähnliche in England.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele bundesländer hat deutschland|wie viele bundesländer gibt es
fakten.a: Deutschland hat 16 Bundesländer.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer war der erste bundeskanzler(?: deutschlands| der bundesrepublik)?
fakten.a: Konrad Adenauer – er war von 1949 bis 1963 der erste Bundeskanzler der Bundesrepublik Deutschland.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wann (?:begann|startete|fing) der erste weltkrieg(?: an)?
fakten.a: Der Erste Weltkrieg begann am 28. Juli 1914, einen Monat nach dem Attentat von Sarajevo.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wann (?:begann|startete|fing) der zweite weltkrieg(?: an)?
fakten.a: Der Zweite Weltkrieg begann am 1. September 1939 mit dem deutschen Überfall auf Polen.

fakten.q: (?:und )?(?:wie heißt|was ist|welcher ist) der höchste berg afrikas|(?:was ist|welcher ist) der höchste berg in afrika
fakten.a: Der Kilimandscharo in Tansania – mit 5.895 m der höchste Berg Afrikas.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele herzen hat (?:ein|der) (?:oktopus|krake)
fakten.a: Drei! Zwei pumpen Blut durch die Kiemen, eins durch den restlichen Körper.

fakten.q: (?:und )?(?:welcher planet ist der sonne am nächsten|was ist der sonnennächste planet)
fakten.a: Merkur ist der Planet, der der Sonne am nächsten ist.

fakten.q: (?:und )?(?:was|welches) ist das schnellste landtier|welches tier ist (?:an land )?am schnellsten
fakten.a: Der Gepard – auf kurzen Strecken schafft er rund 100 km/h.

fakten.q: (?:und )?welches land hat die meisten (?:einwohner|menschen)|was ist das bevölkerungsreichste land(?: der welt)?
fakten.a: Indien – rund 1,43 Milliarden Menschen. Laut UN-Schätzung hat es 2023 China (rund 1,41 Milliarden) überholt.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer hat (?:die )?neunte (?:sinfonie|symphonie) (?:komponiert|geschrieben)
fakten.a: Ludwig van Beethoven – seine Neunte (1824) endet mit der „Ode an die Freude“, heute die Europahymne.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer war der erste mensch im (?:weltall|weltraum|all)
fakten.a: Juri Gagarin – am 12. April 1961 umrundete er mit Wostok 1 einmal die Erde.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele zähne hat (?:ein )?erwachsener(?: mensch)?
fakten.a: Ein Erwachsener hat 32 Zähne, wenn alle Weisheitszähne da sind – sonst 28.

fakten.q: (?:und )?was ist das größte organ des menschen|welches ist das größte organ
fakten.a: Die Haut – bei Erwachsenen rund 2 m² groß und etwa 4 kg schwer. (Das größte innere Organ ist die Leber.)

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele monde hat (?:der )?mars
fakten.a: Der Mars hat zwei kleine Monde: Phobos und Deimos.

fakten.q: (?:und )?(?:was|welches) ist die größte insel(?: der welt)?
fakten.a: Grönland – rund 2,17 Millionen km². (Australien zählt als Kontinent.)

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie viele sekunden hat eine stunde
fakten.a: Eine Stunde hat 3.600 Sekunden (60 × 60).

fakten.q: (?:und )?wer war der erste römische kaiser
fakten.a: Augustus (Octavian) – erster römischer Kaiser von 27 v. Chr. bis 14 n. Chr.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wofür steht dna|was bedeutet dna
fakten.a: DNA steht für Desoxyribonukleinsäure (englisch deoxyribonucleic acid).

fakten.q: (?:und )?was ist h2o
fakten.a: H₂O ist Wasser – zwei Wasserstoffatome und ein Sauerstoffatom.

fakten.q: (?:und )?wie weit ist der mond (?:von der erde )?(?:weg|entfernt)
fakten.a: Der Mond ist im Schnitt etwa 384.400 km von der Erde entfernt – Licht braucht dafür rund 1,3 Sekunden.

superlativ.größte planet: Der größte Planet ist Jupiter – etwa elfmal so breit wie die Erde.
superlativ.kleinste planet: Der kleinste Planet ist Merkur – nur etwa 4.880 km breit.
superlativ.größte ozean: Der größte Ozean ist der Pazifik – etwa 165 Millionen km², rund ein Drittel der Erdoberfläche.
superlativ.größte kontinent: Der größte Kontinent ist Asien – rund 44 Millionen km².
superlativ.größte tier: Das größte Tier ist der Blauwal – bis zu 30 Meter lang und schwerer als jeder Dinosaurier.
superlativ.größte wüste: Die größte Wüste ist die Antarktis (Wüste heißt: kaum Niederschlag); die größte heiße Wüste ist die Sahara.

work_people: If it keeps bothering you, a calm one-on-one usually helps: describe the specific thing that happened and how it affected you, rather than the person.
Write down what exactly bothered you while it's fresh — it makes a later conversation much easier, and sometimes it shows the issue is smaller than it felt.
Give it a night before reacting. If it still matters tomorrow, talk to them directly; if it keeps happening, someone you trust at work or HR can help.
people: When you're both calm, try telling them how it made you feel — “I felt hurt when…” lands better than “You always…”.
Give it a little time, then talk it through face to face. Most conflicts with people we care about get smaller once both sides feel heard.
Ask yourself what you'd need from them to feel okay again — then tell them that, plainly and kindly.
heartbreak: Be kind to yourself — heartbreak really hurts. Lean on friends or family, keep some routine, and give yourself time. It does get easier.
Try not to make big decisions right now. Talk to people who care about you, get outside a little each day, and let yourself feel sad when you need to.
It's okay to grieve the relationship. Maybe take a break from their social media for a while — distance helps the healing.
grief: There's nothing to fix about grief — it's love with nowhere to go. Let yourself feel it, and lean on the people around you.
Take it one day at a time. Sharing memories with others who knew them can help, and so can simply resting.
Be patient with yourself. If it ever feels too heavy to carry, talking to a counsellor or your doctor can really help.
sleep: When sleep won't come: put the phone away, get up for 15 minutes and do something calm in dim light, then try again. Writing down what's on your mind first can help switch it off.
Try slow breathing — in for 4, hold for 4, out for 6 — and don't check the clock. If thoughts keep coming, jot them down for tomorrow; your brain can let go once they're on paper.
tired: Honestly? Rest. Eat something proper, drink some water, and give yourself an early night — tomorrow is a fresh start.
Take a real break: twenty minutes with no screens, maybe a short walk. Then do one small thing that's easy to finish.
Don't try to fix everything tonight. Pick the one thing that can't wait, do it, and let the rest go until tomorrow.
stress: Try this: write down everything on your mind, then circle the one thing you can actually do today. The list feels much smaller afterwards.
A few slow breaths help more than they sound — in for four seconds, hold four, out for four, hold four. Then tackle one small task.
Break it into the next tiny step. You don't need to solve the whole thing right now, just the next part.
sad: Be gentle with yourself today. Reaching out to someone you trust — even a short message — can help more than you'd expect.
It's okay to have a bad day. Do something kind for yourself: a walk, a favourite song, a good meal. And if it keeps weighing on you, talking to someone helps.
Be gentle with yourself today. A short walk, some music, or talking to someone you trust can help a bit.
Sometimes it helps to name what's weighing on you — and to do one small, kind thing for yourself.
failure: One result doesn't define you. Find out where it went wrong, make a plan for next time, and give yourself credit for trying.
Take a breath first. Then look at what you can learn from it — and what you'd do differently. Most people who succeed failed first.
One setback doesn't define you. What would you do differently next time?
That's frustrating — but it's also information. What's one thing you learned from it?
career: Before you decide, write down what you'd miss and what you wouldn't — and what you'd want from the next job. If the list of “wouldn't miss” is long, start looking quietly before you quit.
It's worth asking: is it the job, the people, or the workload? Sometimes a talk with your manager or a change of team fixes it; sometimes it's time to move on.
If you can, line up something new first — it takes the pressure off. And talk it through with someone who knows you well.
generic: What would you tell a good friend in the same situation? That's often the best advice for yourself, too.
Break it down: what's the very next small step you could take? Start there.
If it's not urgent, sleep on it — things often look clearer in the morning.

tips_head: A few things that help most people:

fitness: Start small: three short sessions a week beat one huge one you can't keep up.
Mix strength (twice a week) with something that gets your heart rate up.
Protein with every meal and enough sleep make a bigger difference than most people think.
Track it — even a note on your phone — so you can see your progress.
learning: Practise a little every day instead of a lot once a week.
Learn by doing: a small project or real conversations stick better than reading alone.
Find a partner or a group — it keeps you motivated.
money: Pay yourself first: move a fixed amount to savings right after payday.
Check your subscriptions — they add up quietly.
Give your savings a name and a goal, it makes them easier to protect.
sleep: Same bedtime and wake-up time every day, even on weekends.
No screens for the last half hour before bed.
Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and skip caffeine after lunch.
habit: Pick a start date and tell someone — it makes it real.
Replace the habit with something else instead of just stopping.
Expect slip-ups; one bad day doesn't undo the progress.

coffee: Health agencies say up to about 400 mg of caffeine a day — roughly four cups of filter coffee — is fine for most healthy adults. So that's around the upper limit. Less if it messes with your sleep!
sleep: Most adults need about 7 to 9 hours a night. Regularly much less than that tends to catch up with you.
water: A common guideline is around 2 to 3 litres of fluid a day for adults, more when it's hot or you exercise — and food counts too.
screen: There's no magic number, but if it eats into sleep, work or time with people, it's probably worth cutting back a little.
steps: Around 7,000 to 10,000 steps a day is a common goal — but every bit more than usual already helps.

pineapple: The great pizza debate! I'll stay diplomatic: sweet and salty is a classic combination — and fun fact, the Hawaiian pizza was invented in Canada. Team pineapple or team no-pineapple?
cats_dogs: Both have their fans! Dogs are loyal goofballs, cats are independent little roommates. Which are you?
tea_coffee: Tough one! Coffee for a kick, tea for something gentler — and plenty of people drink both. What's your go-to?
books_movies: Usually the book has more detail, but a great film can surprise you. Do you have one where the movie was better?
summer_winter: Summer for long evenings, winter for cosy nights in. Which season is yours?
beach_mountains: Beach for doing nothing, mountains for views and fresh air. Where would you rather be right now?
early_late: Morning people get the quiet hours, night owls get the late ones. Which one are you?
iphone_android: Both do the job well — it mostly comes down to what you're used to. What do you use?

debate_why: Mostly because tastes really differ, and there's no wrong answer. What's your reason?
Honestly, I just like that people get so passionate about it! Why do you feel that way?
thanks_praise: You deserve it — really well done.

dinner: For a celebration dinner, smart-casual is a safe bet: nice trousers or a skirt and a shirt or top you feel good in. And something comfortable enough to enjoy the evening!
interview: One notch smarter than what people wear there day to day — clean, comfortable and nothing distracting. When in doubt, go slightly more formal.
wedding: Check the invitation for a dress code first. Otherwise a suit or a nice dress works — and avoid white, that's the couple's colour.
date: Something you feel good and comfortable in — confidence matters more than the outfit. Maybe one step up from everyday.
funeral: Dark, simple and modest — black, navy or grey. Nobody will mind if it's plain.
rain: For rain: a waterproof jacket with a hood beats an umbrella when it's windy, plus shoes that can handle puddles — no suede! Layers underneath, so you don't overheat indoors.
cold: For the cold: layers! A warm base, a jumper and a proper coat, plus hat, scarf and gloves. Warm socks make a huge difference.
hot: For the heat: light, loose clothes in linen or cotton, light colours, sunglasses and a hat. And sunscreen!
snow: For snow: waterproof boots with grip, warm layers, a hat and gloves. Being dry is what keeps you warm.
office: Look at what others there wear and go one step tidier for the first days. Comfortable shoes help too!
none: Depends on the occasion — what's it for?

distance_none: I can't measure distances between places — I don't have map data, and I'd rather not guess. A map app will know exactly.
thought_it_was: Easy mix-up! But as far as my sources go, it's {y}, not {x}.
A lot of people think {x} — but it's actually {y}.
puzzled: Sorry, that wasn't clear! Which part should I explain differently?
Oops, I lost you there. What did you mean?

Congratulations on the new {x}! What did you name them?
pet_breed: A {x} — lovely! They're such great companions.
wish_luck: Fingers crossed for you — you'll do great!
pet_young: Aww, {x} — a real baby! Lots of cuddles and chewed socks ahead.
So little! {x} is such a sweet age.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how many moons does mars have

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:what(?:'s| is) the |which is the )?(?:largest|biggest) island(?: in the world| on earth)?

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:what(?:'s| is) the |which is the )?deepest ocean(?: in the world| on earth)?

common.a: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, during the Peaceful Revolution in East Germany.

follow.a: Mass protests in East Germany, people fleeing via Hungary and Czechoslovakia, and reforms in the Soviet Union under Gorbachev. On 9 November an official mistakenly announced that travel was allowed immediately, and crowds forced the border open that night.
Helmut Kohl was Chancellor of West Germany then. He went on to lead reunified Germany from October 1990.
About 28 years: it went up on 13 August 1961 and fell on 9 November 1989.

common.q: (?:and |but |so )?(?:why (?:not|isn'?t it|isn'?t the capital) sydney|why isn'?t sydney the capital(?: of australia)?|why is canberra the capital(?: of australia)?(?: and not sydney)?)
common.a: Because Sydney and Melbourne both wanted to be the capital. In 1908 the compromise was a new city between them — Canberra was built from scratch for it, and Parliament moved there in 1927.
common.v: a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne
common.de: Weil Sydney und Melbourne beide Hauptstadt werden wollten. Der Kompromiss von 1908 war eine neue Stadt zwischen ihnen – Canberra wurde dafür eigens gebaut, das Parlament zog 1927 dorthin.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:what|which) planet is (?:known as |called |nicknamed )?the red planet|why is mars (?:called )?the red planet|why is mars red
common.a: Mars is the Red Planet — its surface is covered in iron-rich dust that has rusted, which gives it that reddish colour.

common.q: (?:and |so )?who (?:invented|made|built) (?:the )?(?:first )?telescope|who was the inventor of the telescope
common.a: The telescope is usually credited to Hans Lipperhey (also spelled Lippershey), a Dutch spectacle-maker who applied for a patent in 1608 — Jacob Metius and Zacharias Janssen made similar claims. Galileo built a much better one in 1609 and pointed it at the sky.
common.de: Als Erfinder des Fernrohrs gilt meist Hans Lipperhey (auch Lippershey), ein niederländischer Brillenmacher, der 1608 ein Patent beantragte – Jacob Metius und Zacharias Janssen erhoben ähnliche Ansprüche. Galileo baute 1609 ein deutlich besseres und richtete es auf den Himmel.

common.q: (?:and |so )?who(?:'s| is) (?:the )?(?:ceo|boss|head|chief executive) of tesla(?: now| currently)?

common.q: (?:and |so )?how old is (?:the )?earth|what(?:'s| is) the age of (?:the )?earth

common.de: Etwa 4,54 Milliarden Jahre – das zeigen die ältesten Meteoriten und Gesteine.

common.q: (?:and |so )?when was (?:the )?berlin wall (?:built|put up|erected|constructed)|when did they build (?:the )?berlin wall
common.a: The Berlin Wall went up on 13 August 1961, almost overnight, to stop people leaving East Germany — it fell on 9 November 1989.
common.de: Die Berliner Mauer wurde am 13. August 1961 gebaut, fast über Nacht, um die Flucht aus der DDR zu stoppen – sie fiel am 9. November 1989.

common.q: (?:and |so )?who painted (?:the )?sistine chapel(?: ceiling)?|who painted the ceiling of (?:the )?sistine chapel

common.q: (?:and |so )?who invented (?:the )?steam engine

common.q: (?:and |so )?where is (?:mount )?kilimanjaro|in which country is (?:mount )?kilimanjaro

common.a: Friedrich Merz has been Chancellor of Germany since 6 May 2025 (as of my data).
common.de: Friedrich Merz ist seit dem 6. Mai 2025 Bundeskanzler (Stand meiner Daten).

common.q: (?:and |so |but )?did (?:albert )?einstein (?:win|get|receive) (?:a|the) nobel prize|(?:and |so )?when did (?:albert )?einstein (?:win|get) (?:a|the|his) nobel prize
common.a: Yes — Albert Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not for relativity but for explaining the photoelectric effect.
common.de: Ja – Albert Einstein bekam 1921 den Nobelpreis für Physik, allerdings nicht für die Relativitätstheorie, sondern für die Erklärung des photoelektrischen Effekts.

common.q: (?:and |so |but )?did marie curie (?:win|get|receive) (?:a|the) nobel prize
common.a: Yes, twice: the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics (with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. She was the first person to win two.
common.de: Ja, sogar zweimal: 1903 den Nobelpreis für Physik (mit Pierre Curie und Henri Becquerel) und 1911 den für Chemie. Sie war der erste Mensch mit zwei Nobelpreisen.

common.q: (?:and |so )?who (?:designed|built|planned|engineered|made) (?:the )?eiffel tower
common.a: The Eiffel Tower was built by Gustave Eiffel's company. The design came from his engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, and the architect Stephen Sauvestre shaped its look.
common.de: Gebaut hat den Eiffelturm die Firma von Gustave Eiffel. Entworfen haben ihn seine Ingenieure Maurice Koechlin und Émile Nouguier, die Gestaltung stammt vom Architekten Stephen Sauvestre.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:has anyone|did anyone|has anybody|did people|have people) (?:ever )?(?:climbed|reached the (?:top|summit) of|been to the top of) (?:mount )?everest|who (?:was the first (?:person |man |one )?to climb|first climbed|first reached the summit of) (?:mount )?everest
common.a: Yes — Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to reach the summit, on 29 May 1953. Thousands have climbed it since.
common.first: Edmund Hillary from New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa from Nepal — they reached the top together on 29 May 1953.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?mercury|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?mercury|how wide is mercury|how big is mercury compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Mercury is about 4,879 km across — about 38% of Earth's width — the smallest planet.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is mercury from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and mercury|mercury (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Mercury is on average about 58 million km (0.39 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?venus|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?venus|how wide is venus|how big is venus compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Venus is about 12,104 km across — almost exactly Earth's size (95%).

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is venus from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and venus|venus (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Venus is on average about 108 million km (0.72 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?mars|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?mars|how wide is mars|how big is mars compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Mars is about 6,779 km across — about half the width of Earth.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is mars from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and mars|mars (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Mars is on average about 228 million km (1.52 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?jupiter|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?jupiter|how wide is jupiter|how big is jupiter compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Jupiter is about 139,820 km across — about 11 times wider than Earth — the largest planet.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is jupiter from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and jupiter|jupiter (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Jupiter is on average about 778 million km (5.2 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?saturn|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?saturn|how wide is saturn|how big is saturn compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Saturn is about 116,460 km across — about 9 times wider than Earth (without its rings).

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is saturn from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and saturn|saturn (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Saturn is on average about 1.43 billion km (9.6 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?uranus|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?uranus|how wide is uranus|how big is uranus compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Uranus is about 50,724 km across — about 4 times wider than Earth.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is uranus from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and uranus|uranus (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Uranus is on average about 2.87 billion km (19.2 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?neptune|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?neptune|how wide is neptune|how big is neptune compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Neptune is about 49,244 km across — almost 4 times wider than Earth.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is neptune from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and neptune|neptune (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Neptune is on average about 4.5 billion km (30 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the planet )?pluto|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the planet )?pluto|how wide is pluto|how big is pluto compared to (?:the )?earth)
common.a: Pluto is about 2,377 km across — smaller than our Moon — it's a dwarf planet.

common.q: (?:and |so )?how far (?:away )?is pluto from the sun|what(?:'s| is) the distance (?:between|from) (?:the sun and pluto|pluto (?:and|to) the sun)
common.a: Pluto is on average about 5.9 billion km (39.5 AU) from the Sun.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is the sun|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of the sun)
common.a: The Sun is about 1.39 million km across — roughly 109 times the width of Earth.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:how (?:big|large) is (?:the )?moon|what(?:'s| is) the (?:size|diameter) of (?:the )?moon)
common.a: The Moon is about 3,474 km across — a bit more than a quarter of Earth's width.

common.q: (?:so )?how many continents (?:are there|(?:are|is) there in the world|does the (?:world|earth) have)
common.a: There are seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America and South America.

common.q: how many oceans (?:are there|does the (?:world|earth) have)(?: in the world)?
common.a: There are five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic Ocean.

common.q: how many planets (?:are there |are )?(?:in (?:our|the) solar system|are there)
common.a: There are eight planets in our solar system: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

common.q: how many legs (?:does|do) (?:a |an )?spiders? have
common.a: Spiders have eight legs.

common.q: how many legs (?:does|do) (?:an? )?insects? have
common.a: Insects have six legs.

common.q: how many players (?:are )?(?:on|in) (?:a |one )?(?:soccer|football) team
common.a: A football (soccer) team has eleven players on the field, including the goalkeeper.

common.q: how many players (?:are )?(?:on|in) (?:a |one )?basketball team
common.a: A basketball team has five players on the court.

common.q: how many bones (?:are )?(?:in|does) (?:the |an adult )?(?:adult )?human body(?: have)?
common.a: An adult human has 206 bones (babies are born with around 270, some of which fuse).

common.q: how many teeth (?:does an adult|do adults|does a human) have
common.a: Adults usually have 32 teeth, including the wisdom teeth.

common.q: how many hearts (?:does|do) (?:an |the )?octopus(?:es)? have
common.a: An octopus has three hearts.

common.q: how many days (?:are )?(?:in|does) a week(?: have)?
common.a: A week has seven days.

common.q: how many hours (?:are )?(?:in|does) a day(?: have)?
common.a: A day has 24 hours.

common.q: what(?:'s| is) the boiling point of water
common.a: Water boils at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level — a bit lower up in the mountains.

common.q: what(?:'s| is) the freezing point of water|at what temperature does water freeze
common.a: Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F).

common.q: what(?:'s| is) the speed of light|how fast is light|how fast does light travel
common.a: Light travels at about 299,792 km per second in a vacuum — roughly 300,000 km/s.

common.q: is (?:a )?tomato(?:es)? (?:a )?fruits?(?: or (?:a )?vegetables?)?|is (?:a )?tomato(?:es)? (?:a )?vegetables?
common.a: Botanically, yes — a tomato is a fruit, because it grows from the flower and holds the seeds. In the kitchen it's usually treated as a vegetable.

common.q: what(?:'s| is) bigger,? the sun or the earth|is the sun bigger than the earth|what(?:'s| is) bigger,? the earth or the sun
common.a: The Sun, by far: it's about 109 times wider than Earth, and more than a million Earths would fit inside it.

common.q: who invented the (?:light ?bulb|lightbulb|incandescent light bulb)
common.a: Many inventors worked on it, but Thomas Edison's carbon-filament bulb of 1879 was the first practical, long-lasting one; Joseph Swan built a similar bulb in England at the same time.

common.q: (?:and |so )?(?:what(?:'s| is) the (?:largest|biggest) planet(?: in (?:our|the) solar system)?|which planet is the (?:largest|biggest)|which is the (?:largest|biggest) planet)
common.a: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system — more than 11 times wider than Earth.

follow.a: It formed early, beyond the 'snow line' where ice was plentiful, so its core grew fast and pulled in huge amounts of hydrogen and helium before the young Sun blew the gas away. It's a gas giant — mostly gas, with no solid surface.
About 95 known moons — and the count keeps growing. The four big ones, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, were discovered by Galileo in 1610; Ganymede is even bigger than Mercury.
No — Jupiter has no solid ground, crushing pressure, deadly radiation and storms bigger than Earth. Some of its moons are more interesting: Europa probably has an ocean under its ice.

Mars is the most realistic option: a solid surface, a day of 24.6 hours and water ice. But the air is thin and mostly CO₂, it's around −60 °C on average and there's lots of radiation — people would need sealed habitats.

common.q: what(?:'s| is) the fastest (?:land )?animal(?: in the world| on earth)?
common.a: The cheetah is the fastest land animal — up to about 100–120 km/h in short sprints. (The fastest of all is the peregrine falcon in a dive.)

common.q: what(?:'s| is) the (?:tallest|biggest) animal(?: in the world| on earth)?
common.a: The tallest animal is the giraffe; the biggest is the blue whale.

common.q: why is the sky blue
common.a: Sunlight is scattered by the air, and blue light is scattered much more than red light because of its shorter wavelength — so blue comes at us from all over the sky.

common.q: why do cats pur+
common.a: Cats mostly purr when they're relaxed and content, but also to calm themselves when stressed or hurt; the sound comes from rapid twitching of the muscles in the voice box.

common.q: how long does it take to learn (?:a (?:new )?language|spanish|french|italian|portuguese|german|english)
common.a: For everyday conversations, most people need roughly 6–12 months of regular practice. To reach a professional level, the US Foreign Service Institute estimates about 600–750 class hours for languages close to English like Spanish, French or Italian (German about 900).

common.q: how many days (?:are )?(?:in|does) a leap year(?: have)?
common.a: A leap year has 366 days.

common.q: who (?:was|is) the first (?:man|person|human|astronaut|human being) (?:on|to (?:walk|step|land) on|to set foot on) (?:the )?moon|who (?:first )?(?:walked|landed|stepped) on (?:the )?moon(?: first)?
common.a: Neil Armstrong — he stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969 during Apollo 11, aged 38. Buzz Aldrin followed him about 20 minutes later.
common.when: That was on 20 July 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission.
common.then: Neil Armstrong was 38 when he stepped onto the Moon in July 1969 (he was born on 5 August 1930).

common.q: when did (?:we|humans|people|man|the us|america|nasa) (?:first )?(?:land|walk|go) (?:on|to) the moon|when was the (?:first )?moon landing
common.a: The first Moon landing was on 20 July 1969 (Apollo 11), with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin.

common.q: who (?:was|is) the second (?:man|person|human) (?:on|to walk on) the moon
common.a: Buzz Aldrin, who followed Neil Armstrong out of Apollo 11's lunar module on 20 July 1969.
common.then: Buzz Aldrin was 39 at the Moon landing in July 1969 (born 20 January 1930).

common.q: who (?:was|is) the first (?:man|person|human|human being) in space|who (?:first )?went to space first|who was the first astronaut
common.a: Yuri Gagarin — the Soviet cosmonaut orbited Earth on 12 April 1961 in Vostok 1.
common.then: Yuri Gagarin was 27 when he flew into space on 12 April 1961 (born 9 March 1934).

common.q: who (?:was|is) the first woman in space
common.a: Valentina Tereshkova, who flew Vostok 6 on 16 June 1963.
common.then: Valentina Tereshkova was 26 when she flew in June 1963 (born 6 March 1937).

speech_wedding:
Of course! A simple structure that works for a wedding speech:

• Thank everyone for coming and say who you are
• How you know the groom (or bride) — one short, funny story
• Something sincere: what makes them great, and what the partner brings out in them
• A warm word to the couple
• Raise your glass: “To the happy couple!”

Keep it to 3–5 minutes. Tell me their names and a story, and I'll help you word it.

• What it means — the one thing people should remember

howto.title: Boiling an egg
steps: Put the egg in boiling water (lower it in gently with a spoon).
Soft: 6 minutes · medium: 8 minutes · hard: 10–11 minutes.
Move it to cold water for a minute — it peels much more easily.

howto.title: Cooking pasta
steps: Use plenty of water (about 1 litre per 100 g) and salt it well once it boils.
Most dried pasta needs 8–12 minutes — the packet time is a good guide.
Taste a minute before the end: it should be soft but still have a little bite (al dente).
Keep a cup of pasta water before draining — it helps the sauce stick.

howto.title: Cooking rice
howto.yield: One cup of uncooked rice gives about three cups cooked — enough for two to three people as a side.
steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs almost clear.
Use about 1.5 cups of water per cup of white rice (2 for brown).
Bring to a boil, cover, turn the heat to low: 12–15 minutes (brown: 35–40).
Let it rest covered for 5–10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

howto.title: Simple pancakes
howto.yield: That makes about 8 to 10 small pancakes — enough for two hungry people.
steps: Mix 200 g flour, 2 tsp baking powder, a pinch of salt and 1 tbsp sugar.
Whisk in 1 egg, 300 ml milk and 2 tbsp melted butter until just smooth.
Cook small ladlefuls in a lightly buttered pan on medium heat.
Flip when bubbles appear on top — about 1–2 minutes per side.

howto.title: Tips for a new puppy
steps: Take them outside often — after waking up, after eating and after playing — and praise them right away.
Keep a simple routine for food, walks and sleep; puppies sleep 18 hours a day.
Give them chew toys so your shoes stay safe.
Short, positive training sessions (a few minutes) work best — and book a first vet visit for vaccinations.

howto.title: Things that help with a sore throat
steps: Warm drinks — tea with honey and lemon is a classic.
Gargle with warm salt water (half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of water) a few times a day.
Throat lozenges and enough sleep; avoid smoke and very dry air.
See a doctor if it lasts more than a week, you have a high fever, or it's hard to swallow or breathe.

howto.title: Things that help with a headache
steps: Drink a big glass of water — mild dehydration is a common cause.
Rest somewhere quiet and dark, away from screens, for a while.
A cool cloth on your forehead or a short walk in fresh air can help.
A standard painkiller can help if it's okay for you; see a doctor if headaches are severe, sudden or keep coming back.

howto.title: Getting through a cold
steps: Rest as much as you can and drink plenty of fluids.
Warm soup, tea with honey and steam (a hot shower) ease the stuffy feeling.
Saline nose spray helps with a blocked nose.
Most colds pass within a week to ten days — see a doctor if you get a high fever or it lasts much longer.

howto.title: Things that help with a cough
steps: Warm drinks with honey soothe the throat (no honey for babies under one).
Keep the air a bit humid and sleep with your head slightly raised.
Avoid smoke and drink enough water.
See a doctor if it lasts more than three weeks, you cough up blood, or you're short of breath.

howto.title: What helps with a fever
steps: Rest and drink a lot — fever uses up fluids.
Light clothes and a light blanket; a lukewarm (not cold) cloth can feel good.
A standard fever reducer can help if it's okay for you.
See a doctor if it's above 39.5 °C, lasts more than three days, or comes with a stiff neck, rash or confusion.

howto.title: Ways to save money
steps: Write down everything you spend for a month — most people find one or two surprises.
Cancel subscriptions you don't really use, and compare insurance, phone and energy contracts once a year.
Cook more at home and take lunch with you; plan meals so less food gets thrown away.
Move a fixed amount to a savings account right after payday, so you never see it.
Wait 48 hours before any non-essential purchase — often the urge passes.

howto.title: A simple monthly budget
steps: Start with your monthly income after tax.
List fixed costs: rent, bills, insurance, transport, debt payments.
A common rule of thumb is 50/30/20: about 50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings and paying off debt.
Set a weekly amount for groceries and fun, and check in every Sunday.
Tell me your income and rent if you like, and I'll help you do the maths.

howto.title: A quick packing list
steps: Documents first: passport or ID, tickets, bank card, insurance details — and photos of them on your phone.
Phone, charger, power bank and an adapter if the plugs are different.
Clothes for the weather plus one layer more than you think, comfortable shoes, swimwear if there's water.
Toiletries in small sizes, sun cream, any medication you take, and a few plasters.
Tip: lay everything out, then take half the clothes and twice the money.

howto.title: Getting rid of hiccups
steps: Hold your breath for 10–20 seconds, then breathe out slowly — repeat a few times.
Sip a glass of cold water slowly, or swallow a teaspoon of sugar.
Breathe slowly into cupped hands for a minute.
Hiccups that last more than two days are worth mentioning to a doctor.

howto.title: Tying a tie (four-in-hand knot)
steps: Drape the tie around your neck, wide end on your right, hanging about 30 cm lower than the narrow end.
Cross the wide end over the narrow end, then bring it back underneath.
Cross it over the front again, then pull it up through the neck loop from below.
Push it down through the front loop you just made and tighten gently, sliding the knot up.

howto.title: How much water to drink
steps: A common guide is about 2–2.5 litres of fluids a day for adults — more when it's hot or you exercise.
Food and other drinks count too.
Pale yellow urine is a simple sign you're drinking enough.

howto.title: Making friends as an adult
steps: Go where the same people show up regularly: a class, a club, a sports team, volunteering.
Repetition matters more than first impressions — keep going for a few weeks.
Be the one who suggests something small: a coffee, a walk, a game night.
Follow up: remembering a detail someone told you goes a long way.

howto.title: What to wear to a job interview
steps: Dress one step smarter than people at the company usually do.
Clean, well-fitting, simple: neutral colours, nothing distracting.
When in doubt: smart trousers or skirt, a shirt or blouse, a blazer and clean shoes.
Lay it out the evening before so the morning is calm.

howto.title: Getting over a cold
steps: Rest, and drink plenty — warm drinks soothe the throat.
Honey with warm water or tea can calm a cough (not for babies under one).
Saltwater gargles help a sore throat.
See a doctor if you have trouble breathing, a high fever for several days, or it lasts over two weeks.

howto.title: Easing a headache
steps: Drink a big glass of water — dehydration is a common cause.
Rest in a quiet, dim room and take a break from screens.
A cool cloth on the forehead or a short walk in fresh air can help.
Sudden, very severe or unusual headaches need a doctor right away.

howto.title: Saving money
steps: Move a fixed amount to savings right after payday — before you can spend it.
Track your spending for one month; the leaks are usually small and regular.
Cancel subscriptions you don't use and compare insurance or phone contracts once a year.
Give your savings a goal — it makes them easier to protect.

howto.title: Studying effectively
steps: Test yourself instead of rereading — recalling is what makes it stick.
Spread it out: short sessions over several days beat one long cram.
Work in 25–50 minute blocks with short breaks, phone in another room.
Explain the topic in your own words; gaps show up immediately.

howto.title: Falling asleep
steps: Same bedtime and wake-up time every day, also at weekends.
No screens for the last 30–60 minutes; keep the room cool and dark.
If you lie awake for more than ~20 minutes, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.
Skip caffeine after lunch and heavy meals late in the evening.

howto.title: Removing a stain
steps: Act quickly and blot — don't rub, or it spreads.
Rinse from the back of the fabric with cold water (hot water sets protein stains like blood).
Dab on a little washing-up liquid or stain remover, leave for 10 minutes, then wash as usual.
Check it's gone before drying — heat makes stains permanent.

howto.title: Unclogging a drain
steps: Pour a kettle of hot (not boiling, for plastic pipes) water down first.
Try a plunger: cover the overflow hole and plunge firmly 10–15 times.
Or half a cup of baking soda, then a cup of vinegar, wait 15 minutes, flush with hot water.
Still blocked? Clean the trap under the sink, or call a plumber.

howto.title: Ironing a shirt
steps: Iron while the shirt is slightly damp, on the setting for its fabric.
Order: collar, cuffs, sleeves, then the back and the two front panels.
Hang it straight away on a hanger and do up the top button.

howto.title: Making good coffee
steps: Use freshly ground beans: about 60 g coffee per litre of water.
Water just off the boil (about 93–96 °C), not boiling.
French press: 4 minutes, then press slowly; filter: pour in slow circles.
Too bitter? Grind coarser or brew shorter. Too sour? Finer or longer.

howto.title: Getting motivated
steps: Make the first step tiny — two minutes is enough to get started.
Decide when and where you'll do it, not just what.
Track streaks: seeing progress is motivating in itself.
Reward yourself after, not before.

howto.title: Calming down
steps: Breathe slowly: in for 4 seconds, hold 4, out for 6 — a few rounds.
Name what's stressing you; writing it down makes it smaller.
Move: a 10-minute walk lowers stress noticeably.
Pick one small thing you can do now, and do just that.

howto.title: Losing weight sensibly
steps: Aim for slow, steady progress — about 0.5 kg a week is sustainable.
Protein and vegetables at every meal keep you full longer.
Watch drinks: juice, soda and alcohol add up quickly.
Walk more and sleep enough — both matter more than people expect.

howto.title: Speaking in front of people
steps: Practise out loud at least three times — once in front of someone.
Know your first two sentences by heart; the rest will follow.
Slow down and pause — it feels long to you, not to the audience.
Look at a few friendly faces, one at a time.

howto.title: Keeping houseplants alive
steps: Most die from too much water: water when the top 2–3 cm of soil is dry.
Use pots with drainage holes and empty the saucer.
Check the light: most houseplants like bright, indirect light.
Feed lightly in spring and summer, rarely in winter.

pain: Totally normal at the start — your fingertips are building calluses. Short sessions (15–20 minutes) a few times a day help, and after 2–3 weeks it gets much better. Take a break if it really hurts.
hard: Everyone feels that at first — chord changes are clumsy for weeks, then suddenly they click. Practise just two chords back and forth for a few minutes a day; it adds up fast.
how_long: With 15–30 minutes a day, most people play simple songs after 2–3 months and feel fairly comfortable after about a year. Regular short practice beats long sessions once a week.
songs: Good beginner songs: “Knockin' on Heaven's Door” (G, D, Am, C), “Horse with No Name” (two chords!), “Stand by Me”, “Three Little Birds” and “Wonderwall” with a capo. Start with the one you like most — motivation matters more than difficulty.
tips: A few things that help: practise a little every day, use a metronome slowly, learn songs you love, and record yourself now and then — you'll hear the progress.

how_long: With regular practice (20–30 minutes a day), simple pieces are possible after a few months, and many people play comfortably after a year or two.
songs: Nice starter pieces: “Heart and Soul”, the first part of “Für Elise”, “Let It Be” (simplified), “River Flows in You” (easy version) and “Ode to Joy”.
tips: Practise slowly and with a steady rhythm, little and often, and learn to read simple sheet music early — it pays off later.

start: Drums — that's so much fun! Do you have a kit at home or a practice pad?

tips: Use a metronome from day one, start slow, and protect your ears — earplugs make a big difference.

presentation:
For the presentation:

• Write down your three key points — everything else supports them
• Practise out loud at least three times, once in front of someone
• Know your first two sentences by heart
• Check the tech and your slides the day before
• Sleep well the night before — it matters more than one more run-through

Want help with the opening?
interview:
For the interview:

• Read up on the company and the role — know why you want it
• Prepare three short stories about things you achieved
• Have two or three questions for them ready
• Pick your outfit and route the day before

You'll do great!
exam:
For the exam:

• Make a plan: which topics on which day
• Practise with old questions instead of only re-reading
• Short breaks every 45–60 minutes
• Sleep well the night before — no all-nighter

What subject is it?
meeting:
For the meeting:

• Know what you want to get out of it — one sentence
• Jot down your key points and any numbers you need
• Think about the questions others might ask

That's usually enough to feel prepared.
date:
For the date:

• Pick a place where you can talk — not too loud
• Have a couple of easy questions in mind (travel, food, weekends)
• Wear something you feel good in
• And remember: they're probably just as nervous!

italian.name: Spaghetti carbonara
steps: Cook the spaghetti in well-salted water.
Whisk 2 eggs plus 1 yolk with plenty of grated parmesan and black pepper.
Fry diced pancetta or bacon until crisp.
Drain the pasta (keep a cup of the water), toss it with the pancetta off the heat.
Stir in the egg mix quickly, adding a splash of pasta water until creamy — no scrambled eggs!

italian.name: Mushroom risotto
steps: Soften a chopped onion in butter, add 300 g risotto rice and toast for a minute.
Add a splash of white wine and let it cook away.
Add hot stock one ladle at a time, stirring, for about 18 minutes.
Fry sliced mushrooms separately and stir them in.
Finish with butter and parmesan, rest 2 minutes, serve.

italian.name: Homemade margherita pizza
steps: Mix 500 g flour, 7 g yeast, 1 tsp salt and 325 ml warm water; knead 10 minutes.
Let it rise for 1–2 hours.
Stretch it thin, spread tomato sauce, add mozzarella.
Bake as hot as your oven goes (250 °C+) for 8–10 minutes.
Top with fresh basil and a little olive oil.

mexican.name: Chicken tacos
steps: Slice chicken and season with cumin, paprika, chilli, salt and lime.

Fill with chicken, salsa, avocado and a squeeze of lime.

mexican.name: Bean burritos
steps: Fry onion and garlic, add black beans, cumin and a little water; mash lightly.
Cook some rice.
Fill large tortillas with rice, beans, cheese and salsa.
Roll them up and toast in a pan until golden.

mexican.name: Guacamole with nachos
steps: Mash 2 ripe avocados.
Mix in lime juice, salt, finely chopped onion, tomato and coriander.
Serve right away with tortilla chips.

indian.name: Chickpea curry
steps: Fry onion, garlic and ginger in oil.
Add curry powder or garam masala and cook for a minute.
Add a tin of tomatoes, a tin of chickpeas and a little coconut milk.
Simmer 15–20 minutes, season, serve with rice or naan.

indian.name: Butter chicken
steps: Marinate chicken in yoghurt, garam masala and garlic.
Fry it, then set aside.
Make a sauce of butter, onion, tomato passata and spices; simmer 10 minutes.
Add cream and the chicken, simmer 10 more minutes, serve with rice.

indian.name: Dal
steps: Rinse 200 g red lentils.
Simmer them with turmeric and water for about 20 minutes until soft.
Fry garlic, cumin seeds and chilli in oil and pour it over.
Season with salt and lemon.

japanese.name: Teriyaki salmon
steps: Mix soy sauce, mirin and a little sugar.
Fry the salmon skin-side down until crisp, then flip.
Pour in the sauce and let it thicken into a glaze.
Serve with rice and sesame seeds.

japanese.name: Simple ramen
steps: Simmer stock with soy sauce, garlic and ginger.
Cook the noodles separately.
Soft-boil an egg (about 6½ minutes).
Put noodles in a bowl, pour over the broth, top with egg, spring onion and whatever you like.

japanese.name: Homemade sushi bowls
steps: Cook sushi rice and season with rice vinegar, sugar and salt.
Slice salmon or tuna, avocado and cucumber.
Arrange on the rice, top with sesame and soy sauce.

chinese.name: Egg fried rice
steps: Use cooked, cold rice.
Scramble 2 eggs in a hot wok and set aside.
Fry spring onion and garlic, add the rice, fry until hot.
Add soy sauce, peas and the egg, toss and serve.

chinese.name: Kung pao chicken
steps: Dice chicken and coat it with soy sauce and cornflour.
Fry dried chillies and peanuts briefly, then the chicken.
Add a sauce of soy, vinegar, sugar and a little water.
Toss until glossy, serve with rice.

chinese.name: Veggie stir-fry with noodles
steps: Cook the noodles.
Stir-fry sliced vegetables over high heat for 3–4 minutes.
Add garlic, ginger, soy and a little honey.
Toss in the noodles and serve.

thai.name: Thai green curry
steps: Fry 2 tbsp green curry paste in a little oil.
Add coconut milk and bring to a simmer.
Add chicken or tofu and vegetables; cook 10 minutes.
Season with fish sauce and lime, serve with rice.

thai.name: Pad thai
steps: Soak rice noodles.
Fry garlic, then shrimp or tofu, then push aside and scramble an egg.
Add noodles and a sauce of tamarind, fish sauce and sugar.
Toss with bean sprouts, top with peanuts and lime.

greek.name: Chicken souvlaki
steps: Marinate chicken in olive oil, lemon, garlic and oregano.
Thread onto skewers and grill or pan-fry.
Serve in pita with tzatziki, tomato and onion.

greek.name: Greek salad
steps: Chop tomatoes, cucumber, red onion and pepper.
Add olives and a block of feta.
Dress with olive oil and oregano.

french.name: Coq au vin
steps: Brown chicken pieces with bacon.
Add onion, garlic and mushrooms.
Pour in red wine and stock, add thyme.
Simmer about an hour until tender.

french.name: Ratatouille
steps: Dice aubergine, courgette, peppers and onion.
Fry them in olive oil one after another.
Add tomatoes, garlic and herbs; simmer 30 minutes.

dish_which: Which one — {x}? I'll walk you through it.
person_likes_answer: From what you told me, {x} loves {y}.
no_worries_ack: All good! Anything else on your mind?
No problem at all. What else is up?
👍 Just shout if you need anything.
racing_mind: That's so common at night — the brain finally gets quiet time and decides to replay everything. Try writing the thoughts down on paper; once they're out of your head, it's easier to let go.
Ugh, the 3 a.m. thought spiral. A trick that helps many people: jot down what's bothering you and one next step for tomorrow. Then it's handled for tonight.
event_unknown: I've read about the {x}, but the part that answers that isn't in my copy. Want me to tell you what I do know about it?
Hmm, my article on the {x} doesn't say that clearly, so I'd rather not guess. I can tell you what it does say, though.
office_dated: As of my copy of Wikipedia ({z}), the {x} was {y}. That can change, so it's worth a quick check if it matters.
In my copy of Wikipedia ({z}), the {x} is {y} — but offices change, so that may be out of date by now.
office_undated: According to my copy of Wikipedia, the {x} is {y} — offices change, though, so that may be out of date.
tip_try: Hope it helps! Tell me how it went.
Good luck with it — let me know if it works for you.
tip_try_night: Hope it helps. Sleep well when it comes! 🌙
Fingers crossed. Be gentle with yourself — even resting with your eyes closed helps. Good night!
same_fine: Glad to hear it! So, what's on your mind today?
Nice, a good day all round then. Anything you feel like talking about?
bot_not_sad: Ha, maybe a little! But honestly, I don't mind — I get to talk to people like you all day.
Don't worry about me — I can't feel sad either. And I quite like this chat!
moved_work: A new job in {x}, exciting! How are you settling in so far?

moved_study: Studying in {x} — that's a great adventure. How are you finding it so far?

moved_other: That's a big change. How are you finding {x} so far?
