areas_lead:
Popular areas in {x}: {y}

It depends a lot on budget and what you like — quiet, nightlife or green spaces?

In {x}, people often like {y}

What matters most to you — price, nightlife, or being close to work?

areas.berlin: Kreuzberg and Neukölln (lively, bars, international), Prenzlauer Berg (cafés, families, calmer), Friedrichshain (young, nightlife) and Charlottenburg (elegant, quieter, west).
areas.munich: Schwabing (lively, near the English Garden), Maxvorstadt (students, museums), Haidhausen (charming, central) and Sendling (more affordable).
areas.hamburg: Sternschanze and St. Pauli (lively, alternative), Ottensen (cosy, cafés), Eimsbüttel (popular with young families) and Winterhude (green, near the Stadtpark).
areas.frankfurt: Sachsenhausen (apple-wine taverns, by the river), Nordend (cafés, old buildings), Bornheim (village feel) and Bockenheim (students, cheaper).
areas.cologne: Ehrenfeld (creative, nightlife), the Belgian Quarter (bars, boutiques), Südstadt (relaxed, by the Rhine) and Sülz (families, calm).
areas.london: Shoreditch and Hackney (creative, nightlife), Clapham and Brixton (young professionals), Islington (pubs, central) and Greenwich (green, calmer).
areas.paris: Le Marais (central, lively), Canal Saint-Martin (young, cafés), Montmartre (charming, hilly) and Batignolles (village feel, calmer).
areas.new york: Williamsburg (Brooklyn, creative), the East Village (nightlife), Astoria (Queens, good value) and the Upper West Side (calm, by Central Park).
areas.amsterdam: De Pijp (markets, cafés), Jordaan (canals, charming), Oost (green, families) and Noord (creative, cheaper).
areas.vienna: Neubau (creative, shops), Josefstadt (central, calm), Leopoldstadt (Prater park, lively) and Wieden (cafés, near the Naschmarkt).
areas.zurich: Kreis 4 and 5 (lively, nightlife), Wiedikon (relaxed), Seefeld (by the lake, upmarket) and Oerlikon (more affordable).
areas.barcelona: Gràcia (village feel, squares), Eixample (central, elegant), El Born (historic, bars) and Poblenou (near the beach, modern).
areas.madrid: Malasaña (young, bars), Chamberí (classic, calm), La Latina (tapas, historic) and Lavapiés (multicultural, cheaper).
areas.lisbon: Príncipe Real (stylish), Alfama (historic, charming), Campo de Ourique (calm, families) and Cais do Sodré (nightlife).
areas.tokyo: Shimokitazawa (vintage, cafés), Nakameguro (stylish, by the canal), Kichijoji (park, relaxed) and Koenji (alternative, cheaper).
areas.rome: Trastevere (charming, lively), Monti (central, boutiques), Testaccio (food, local) and Prati (calm, near the Vatican).

pet_call: Good idea — better safe than sorry. I hope {x} feels better soon! 🐾
That's the right call. Fingers crossed it's nothing serious — give {x} a cuddle from me.
thanks_nice: Aw, that's kind of you! Happy to help anytime. 😊
Aw, thank you — that made my day! 😊
Thank you — that's lovely to hear. I'm always here if you need me.
exam_subjects: {X} — three big ones! Which one worries you the most?
That's a full week: {x}. Which one do you feel least ready for?
exam_first: I'd start with the one you find hardest, while you're still fresh — or the one that comes first, if it's very soon. Which one is your weakest?
Usually: the earliest exam first, but give the hardest subject the most time. Which one do you find toughest?
exam_worst: Then I'd start with {x} — give it your freshest hours each day, and do the other subjects in the afternoon. Short sessions with old exam questions work best. You've got this!
Start with {x}, then. Do a little every day rather than one big block, and practise with past questions. The subjects you're better at need less time — use them as a break.
wfh_lonely: That makes so much sense — working from home can be really isolating. Whole days go by without talking to anyone face to face.
Ah, yes — home office is great for focus, but it can get really lonely. No colleagues, no small talk by the coffee machine.
maybe_should: That could really help — even small steps count. Want a few ideas?
I think that's a great idea. Starting small is totally fine. Should I suggest a few things?
lonely_ideas:
A few ideas:

• Work from a café or co-working space a day or two a week
• Join something regular — a sports club, a class, a choir, a running group
• Volunteer — you meet people while doing something good
• Message one old friend today, just to say hi

Does any of that sound like you?
ideas_liked: Glad something there sounds good! Even starting with just one of them is a great step.
Nice! Pick the one that feels easiest and give it a go — tell me how it went.
exam_count: {X} exams — no wonder you're stressed. Which subjects are they?
Oof, {x} exams at once is a lot. What are the subjects?
interview_at: {X} — impressive! What's the role? You must have done something right to get this far.
Ooh, {x}! That's exciting. Do you know what the interview will be like — technical, or more of a chat?

weakness: Pick a real but harmless weakness and show what you do about it. For example: “I used to take on too much myself — now I plan my week and ask for help earlier.” Honest, short, and it ends on growth. Avoid fake ones like “I'm a perfectionist”.
strength: Name one or two strengths that fit the job and back each with a short example: “I'm good at explaining complicated things — in my last job I trained all the new colleagues.” Examples beat adjectives.
salary: Know your number before you go in — check typical salaries for the role. If they ask, give a range with your target near the bottom of it, and say you're flexible depending on the whole package.
why: Keep it about them and about the future: what excites you about this company and role, and what you'd bring. Skip anything negative about your old job.

interview_luck_at: Good luck at {x} tomorrow — you've prepared, and you'll do great! 🍀 Tell me how it went.
Fingers crossed for {x}! Breathe, be yourself — they invited you for a reason. 🍀
interview_luck: Good luck tomorrow — you've got this! 🍀 Tell me how it went.
bday_unknown: You haven't told me your birthday yet — when is it?
bday_days: Your birthday is in {x} days — on {y}. 🎉
age_if: You're {x} now, and you'll turn {y} on {z}. 🎂
age_if_nobday: Born in that year, you're {x} or {y} now — {y} once you've had your birthday this year.
food_time_known: The quickest one takes about {x} minutes — the others around 20–30.
food_time: Most of these take about 15–30 minutes, so you'll be eating soon.
trust_betrayed: You're not stupid. Trusting someone you love is exactly what you're supposed to do — the one who broke that trust is him, not you.
Please don't blame yourself. Being able to trust is a good quality. What he did says everything about him and nothing about you.
text_ex: Honestly? I'd wait. Right now you're hurt, and anything you send might not say what you really mean. Give it a few days — and ask yourself what you'd want to get out of it.
I'd give it some time first. If you still want to say something in a few days, you'll say it more calmly. And you don't owe him a reply.
interview_nerves: Totally normal — being nervous means it matters to you. Remember: {x} already liked your application enough to invite you. Prepare two or three stories, get a good night's sleep, and you'll be fine.
Of course you are, that's a big one! Nerves usually fade after the first few minutes. Breathe slowly, and remember it's a conversation — you're checking them out too.
down_vague: That kind of heaviness, where it's not one thing but everything, is really draining. You don't need a reason to feel like this.
Yeah, sometimes it's not one big thing, just everything piling up. That's still real, and it's okay to feel worn down by it.
talk_helps: I'm here, take your time. What have your days been like lately?
Then let's talk. Is there one moment from this week that felt especially heavy?
sarc_monday: Ha, the enthusiasm is overwhelming! 😄 Mondays are rough. Anything nice planned to get you through the week?
Oh yes, everyone's favourite day. 🙃 Hang in there, it gets better from Tuesday.
sarcasm: Ha, I can hear the enthusiasm from here! 😄 That sounds rough.
Sounds like a real highlight. 🙃 Early starts are tough. How are you holding up?
weekend_wish: Same! Hang in there, it'll be here before you know it. Any plans for it?
The weekend can't come soon enough, right? What would make it a good one?
misunderstood: Sorry about that! What did you mean? Try saying it a little differently and I'll do my best.
My bad. Let's try again: what do you need?
help_ask: Of course! What do you need?
Sure, I'm happy to help. What's up?
alarm: I can't set alarms or timers: I don't control your phone or computer. But I can remember things for you. Say “remind me to …” and ask me “what do I need to do?” later.
what_else:
A few more things I'm good at:
• Quizzes, riddles and fun facts
• Recipes and what to cook with what you have
• Book, film and game tips
• Calculations, percentages, time zones and days until a date
• Comparing countries, cities and people (“compare France and Germany”)

What sounds good?
sarcasm_ack: Ha, I figured! 😄 Hang in there. Coffee helps.
Yeah, I didn't think so. 😄 What would make today a bit better?

cost_says.cheap: {X} is fairly affordable compared with most of Western Europe and North America: eating out, public transport and museums won't break the bank.
cost_says.mid: {X} is mid-range: not cheap, but manageable. Hotels in the centre and tourist-trap restaurants add up; small local restaurants, markets and public transport keep it reasonable.
cost_says.pricey: {X} is on the expensive side, especially hotels and eating out in the centre. Booking early, staying a bit further out and eating where locals eat helps a lot.

trip_length: {X} days in {y} is a nice amount: enough for the highlights without rushing. Want a rough plan for the days?
{X} days is perfect for {y}. Should I suggest what to see first?
visa_eu: No: as an EU citizen you can travel to {x} with just your ID card or passport, no visa needed.
visa_check: That depends on the rules for your passport, and they change. Please check the official foreign office website of your country before you go. I'd rather not guess on something this important.
cat_small_flat: Cats usually do fine in small flats, as long as they have things to climb, a window to look out of and someone to play with. Many indoor cats are perfectly happy.
cat_ok: Yes, absolutely. A calm adult cat is often an even better fit for a small flat than a kitten. Shelters can tell you which cats are relaxed indoors.
cat_need:
For a cat you'll need:

• A litter tray, litter and a scoop
• Food and water bowls, and good-quality food
• A scratching post (or two!)
• A carrier for vet visits
• A few toys and a cosy bed

And a first vet check-up after you get it.

pet_names.cat: A few ideas: Luna, Milo, Simba, Nala, Oliver, Mochi, Pepper or Leo. Do you know yet if it'll be a boy or a girl?
pet_names.dog: A few ideas: Max, Bella, Charlie, Luna, Buddy, Daisy, Rocky or Nala. Any idea what kind of dog it'll be?

learn_time: For simple conversations, most people need about 3–6 months of regular practice, say 20–30 minutes a day. Feeling comfortable takes a year or two.
ache_since: Since {x} — that's a long time with a headache. Have you had enough water and something to eat today?
Ugh, since {x}. Have you been staring at a screen a lot, or not drinking much?
ache_water: That might well be it: not drinking enough is one of the most common causes of headaches. Have a big glass of water now and another in the next hour.
ache_meds: Water and a short break from screens first. If it doesn't get better, a common over-the-counter painkiller like ibuprofen or paracetamol can help. Follow the dose on the pack. If it's very sudden and severe, comes with fever, a stiff neck or blurred vision, see a doctor.
ache_ok: Good idea. I hope it eases off soon! 💧
Sounds like a plan. Feel better soon!

spend_on.food: Food is one of the easiest places to save: plan the week's meals, shop with a list (and not hungry!), cook bigger batches and take lunch to work. Eating out once a week less often saves more than you'd think.
spend_on.eating out: Eating out adds up fast. Try cooking on weekdays and keeping restaurants for one special evening a week, and take lunch from home.
spend_on.coffee: A daily café coffee can be 60–100 a month. A good thermos and coffee from home, plus the café as a treat once or twice a week, makes a real difference.
spend_on.clothes: For clothes: a 48-hour rule before buying, unsubscribing from shop newsletters and checking second-hand first helps a lot.
spend_on.shopping: A 48-hour rule before non-essential buys works wonders, and so does deleting saved card details from shopping sites.
spend_on.subscriptions: List every subscription and cancel what you haven't used in the last month. Most people find at least one or two.
spend_on.other: Track that spending for a month, then set a weekly limit for it. Seeing the number usually does half the work.

budget_rule: A popular one is 50/30/20: 50% of your take-home pay for needs (rent, bills, groceries), 30% for wants and 20% for savings or paying off debt. Adjust it to your situation. Even 10% saved is a great start.
credit_stolen: That's so frustrating — and unfair. You did the work and someone else gets the recognition. How long has this been going on?
Ugh, that's one of the most annoying things at work. Does your boss know what you actually contributed?
credit_again: Again? Then it's a pattern, not an accident — it's fair to do something about it.
talk_boss: I think it's reasonable, yes. Keep it factual: what you did, with dates or emails, and ask how to make your contributions more visible. It doesn't have to sound like a complaint about your colleague.
bring_up: Something like: “I'd like to make sure my work is visible. On the X project I did A and B (here's the email). How can we make it clearer who did what in future?” Calm, factual, and focused on the work, not on blame. It also helps to send short recap emails after you finish something.

gift_lead: Since {who} {x}, how about {y}? Personal beats expensive every time.
With {x} in mind: {y}. Add a handwritten card and it's perfect.
gift_budget: Under {x}, still easy: {y}. And a handwritten card costs nothing but means a lot.
decide_ask: That's a tough spot to be in. What are the two options? Tell me what each one has going for it.
decide_tradeoff: The classic one: money versus meaning. A few questions that help: Would the lower salary still cover your life comfortably? Which job would you be proud of in two years? And which one would teach you more?
decide_view: If the lower salary still pays your bills comfortably, I'd lean towards the more interesting one. Interest keeps you motivated, you learn faster, and that usually pays off later too. If money is tight right now, though, the better-paid one is a perfectly good choice.
decide_agree: Sounds like you already knew deep down. Good luck with it! 🍀
run_start: Love it! Running is one of the easiest sports to start: just shoes and a door. Have you run before, or is this a fresh start?
run_beginner: That's totally fine — everyone starts somewhere. The trick is to start slower than you think: walk–run intervals, and you'll be surprised how fast you improve.
run_often: Three times a week is perfect for starting, with a rest day in between so your body can adapt.
run_far: Don't think in distance yet, think in time: 20–30 minutes of alternating 1 minute running and 2 minutes walking. Every week, run a bit more and walk a bit less. In 8–10 weeks most people can run 30 minutes straight.
run_shoes: Proper running shoes matter most, ideally from a running shop where they look at how you run. Comfortable and cushioned beats fashionable. The rest (shorts, a T-shirt that isn't cotton) can be anything.
run_go: Great — go slow, enjoy it, and tell me how the first run went! 🏃
kid_nervous: That's so normal before a test — it shows he cares. How old is he?
Aw, poor thing. Nerves before a test are completely normal. What's he most worried about?
kid_help:
A few things that help:

• A short, relaxed review tonight instead of last-minute cramming
• A good night's sleep and a proper breakfast
• Tell him that mistakes are okay and that you're proud of him for trying
• A simple breathing trick for the test: in for 4, out for 6

Your calm helps him most.
kid_age: At {x}, a calm evening and knowing you're not worried about the grade makes a big difference. Maybe do one or two practice problems together, then something fun to switch off.
guests_ack: Nice, a dinner party! How many people are coming?
guests_count: {X} people — a proper dinner! Any dietary needs, like vegetarian or allergies?
guests_vegan: Good to know. The easiest way is a main everyone can eat, so the {y} guest doesn't get a sad side dish. Want ideas?
guests_menu_vegan:
For a group with a {y} guest:

• A big vegetable and chickpea curry with rice and naan, everyone loves it
• Chili sin carne with all the toppings, guests add what they like
• Pasta with a rich tomato and roasted vegetable sauce

All of them scale easily for {x} and can be made ahead.
guests_menu:
For {x} people, something you can make ahead works best:

• Lasagne or a vegetable lasagne
• A big curry with rice
• A roast chicken with roast vegetables

Then you can enjoy your guests instead of standing at the stove.
guests_time: About an hour, most of it hands-off simmering — and all of them taste even better made a few hours ahead.
dessert_vegan:
Vegan desserts everyone likes:

• Sorbet with fresh berries
• Dark chocolate mousse (many dark chocolates are vegan)
• Baked apples with cinnamon and a crumble topping
• A big fruit platter with melted dark chocolate for dipping
dessert_guests: For dessert: a tiramisu or panna cotta made the day before, or a simple fruit crumble with ice cream.
todo_added: Added: {x}. Ask me “what do I need to do?” any time.
todo_done_all: Nice, ticked off: {x}. ✅ That was everything on your list!
long_week: Oof, long weeks are draining. What made this one so long?
Ugh, one of those weeks. What's been keeping you so busy?
deadlines: Deadlines stacking up are the worst. At least you made it through, and the weekend is close!
That's a lot of pressure. Did you get most of it done?
almost_weekend: Yes! Almost there. 🎉 Any plans for the weekend?
Friday — the finish line is in sight! Doing anything nice this weekend?
bot_weekend: Ha, I'll be right here, reading Wikipedia and waiting for good questions. 😄 What about you, any plans?
Same as always: chatting and reading. My weekends are very relaxed! What are you up to?
hike_plan: Hiking sounds lovely! Do you know where yet, or still looking for a trail?
Oh nice, a hike! Fresh air after a long week is exactly right. Where are you thinking of going?
hike_tips:
A few hiking basics:

• Pick a route a bit shorter than you think, and check the weather in the morning
• Start early, it's cooler and less crowded
• Tell someone where you're going
• Break in your shoes beforehand, no brand-new boots
• Turn around if the weather turns: the mountain will still be there
hike_bring:
For a day hike:

• Water (plenty) and snacks, like nuts, a sandwich, fruit
• Layers: a warm top and a rain jacket, even if it's sunny
• Good shoes with grip
• Sun cream, sunglasses, a cap
• Phone with the map downloaded, plus a power bank
• A small first-aid kit and plasters
hike_water: Roughly half a litre per hour of hiking, more when it's hot or steep. For a 4-hour hike, 2 litres is a good start.
same_again: You've said that a few times now 😄 Everything alright? If you're not sure what to ask, I could tell you a fun fact or quiz you.
Ha, I'm getting déjà vu! 😄 Anything specific on your mind? I'm happy to suggest something.
lang_de: Klar, gern! Ab jetzt reden wir auf Deutsch. Was liegt dir auf dem Herzen?
lang_en: Sure! Let's switch to English. What's on your mind?
numbers_only: {x}, is that a number to calculate, a code, or a cat walking over the keyboard? 😄
bad_day_story: Oh no, that's one of those days where everything goes wrong at once. 😩 I'm really sorry. Is it at least over now, or is there more to get through?
What a day! One thing after another. No wonder you're fed up. Do you want to vent a bit more, or would a distraction help?

ubiquitous: found everywhere, seeming to be present all the time
Smartphones have become ubiquitous: almost everyone has one.
ambiguous: open to more than one meaning; unclear
His answer was ambiguous, so nobody knew if he agreed.
empathy: the ability to understand and share someone else's feelings
She showed real empathy when her friend lost his job.
nostalgia: a sentimental longing for the past
Old songs from school always fill me with nostalgia.
irony: when the opposite of what you expect happens, or saying the opposite of what you mean
The fire station burned down: what irony.
procrastinate: to keep putting off something you should do
I always procrastinate when I have to do my taxes.
resilient: able to recover quickly from difficulties
Children are often more resilient than we think.
sustainable: able to continue without harming the environment or running out
We need more sustainable ways to produce energy.
pragmatic: dealing with things in a practical, realistic way
She took a pragmatic approach and fixed what she could.
cynical: believing that people are mostly selfish or dishonest
After years in politics, he became quite cynical.
eloquent: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing
She gave an eloquent speech at the wedding.
meticulous: very careful and precise about details
He keeps meticulous notes of every meeting.
inevitable: certain to happen, impossible to avoid
With that much rain, flooding was inevitable.

b64.panic_tips:

• Remind yourself: it's a panic attack, it feels awful but it passes, usually within 10–20 minutes.
• Breathe out slowly — longer out than in (in for 4, out for 6–8).
• Ground yourself: name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear.
• Afterwards, be gentle with yourself.

If panic attacks keep coming, a doctor or therapist can really help — they're very treatable.

dish_recipe.carbonara: The Roman way, for two: 200 g spaghetti, 100 g guanciale (or pancetta), 2 eggs plus 1 yolk, 50 g grated pecorino, lots of black pepper. Fry the guanciale until crisp, whisk eggs with pecorino and pepper, toss the drained pasta with the guanciale off the heat, then stir in the egg mix with a splash of pasta water until creamy. No cream — the creaminess comes from eggs, cheese and starch.
dish_recipe.bolognese: Soffritto (onion, carrot, celery) in butter or oil, then minced beef (and pork), a splash of white wine and milk, a little tomato, and then simmer gently for two to three hours. In Bologna it goes with tagliatelle.
dish_recipe.cacio e pepe: Just three things: pecorino romano, black pepper and pasta water. Toast the pepper, add pasta water, then the pasta, and stir in finely grated pecorino off the heat until it turns into a smooth sauce.
dish_recipe.aglio e olio: Spaghetti, plenty of garlic sliced thin, olive oil, chilli flakes and parsley. Gently fry the garlic and chilli in the oil (don't let it brown), toss with the pasta and a splash of pasta water.

paris: Food in Paris: a fresh croissant or pain au chocolat from a boulangerie in the morning, a croque monsieur or steak frites in a bistro, crêpes from a street stand, and macarons or an éclair from a pâtisserie. Tip: the menu du jour at lunch is much cheaper than dinner.
rome: Food in Rome: carbonara, cacio e pepe and amatriciana in a trattoria, pizza al taglio by the slice, supplì (fried rice balls) and gelato. Coffee at the bar counter is cheaper than at a table.
london: Food in London: fish and chips, a full English breakfast, Sunday roast in a pub, and the curries on Brick Lane. Borough Market is great for tasting a bit of everything.
barcelona: Food in Barcelona: tapas like patatas bravas and croquetas, pan con tomate, paella by the sea, and churros with chocolate. Dinner starts late — 9 pm is normal.
lisbon: Food in Lisbon: pastéis de nata (Pastéis de Belém is the famous spot), grilled sardines, bacalhau and a bifana sandwich. Try a ginjinha, the cherry liqueur.
berlin: Food in Berlin: currywurst, döner kebab (Berlin claims it), a big breakfast brunch on the weekend, and lots of great Vietnamese food.
vienna: Food in Vienna: Wiener Schnitzel, Sachertorte in a classic café, apple strudel, and a sausage from a Würstelstand late at night.
amsterdam: Food in Amsterdam: stroopwafels fresh from the market, bitterballen with a beer, raw herring if you're brave, and Dutch pancakes.
tokyo: Food in Tokyo: sushi at a counter, ramen, yakitori under the train tracks, and onigiri from any convenience store — they're surprisingly good. Tipping isn't expected.
new york: Food in New York: a slice of pizza folded in half, a bagel with cream cheese, pastrami at a deli, and a hot dog from a street cart.
other: My best food tip for {x}: eat where the locals eat — small places a street away from the big sights, local markets, and the lunch menus, which are usually cheaper than dinner.

workload_advice:
Here's what often helps:

• Make a quick list of everything on your plate, with rough time estimates.
• Take it to your boss and ask: “Which of these matters most? If I take on the new task, what can wait?”
• That makes the overload visible without sounding like a complaint — and the priorities become their decision, not your stress.

photosynthesis: Plants make their own food from sunlight. They take in water and carbon dioxide, use the Sun's energy to turn them into sugar, and release oxygen as a by-product.
It's the reason we have food and oxygen: almost every food chain starts with plants, and the oxygen we breathe comes from photosynthesis.
gravity: Everything with mass pulls on everything else. The Earth is so heavy that its pull keeps us on the ground and the Moon in orbit.
Without gravity there'd be no planets, no orbits and no atmosphere — it holds the whole universe together.
evolution: Living things slowly change over many generations. Individuals that happen to suit their environment better survive and have more offspring, so their traits spread.
It explains why life is so diverse — and helps medicine, for example in understanding how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics.
democracy: People rule themselves: citizens choose their leaders in free elections and can vote them out again.
It protects people's rights and lets a country change its government peacefully instead of by force.
inflation: Prices go up over time, so the same money buys less. If bread costs €2 this year and €2.10 next year, that's 5% inflation.
It eats into savings and wages, so central banks try to keep it low and steady — around 2% a year.
dna: DNA is the instruction manual inside every cell. It's a long molecule that tells the body how to grow, work and repair itself — and it's passed from parents to children.
It's the basis of heredity, and reading it helps diagnose diseases, solve crimes and develop medicines.
black hole: A place where so much mass is squeezed so tightly that gravity lets nothing escape — not even light.
Black holes shape galaxies (most have a giant one in the middle) and test our theories of gravity in the most extreme conditions.
climate change: The Earth is getting warmer because burning coal, oil and gas adds greenhouse gases to the air, which trap heat like a blanket.
It brings more heatwaves, droughts, floods and rising seas — which affect food, water and where people can live.
electricity: Tiny particles called electrons flowing through a wire, like water through a pipe. That flow can power lights, motors and phones.
Almost everything in modern life runs on it — from fridges and hospitals to the internet.
internet: A huge network of computers all over the world that can send each other data — web pages, messages, videos — in small packets.
It connects billions of people and is how we communicate, work, learn and shop today.
vaccine: A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless preview of a germ, so it learns to recognise and fight it before you ever get really sick.
Vaccines have wiped out smallpox and prevent millions of deaths every year from diseases like measles and polio.
atom: The tiny building blocks of everything. Each atom has a centre (protons and neutrons) with electrons around it.
Everything — you, air, water, stars — is made of atoms, so understanding them explains chemistry, materials and energy.
recession: When a country's economy shrinks for a while — businesses sell less, and people lose jobs. Often defined as two quarters in a row of falling output.
It affects jobs, wages and savings, which is why governments and central banks try to soften it.
blockchain: A shared digital record book copied across many computers. New entries are linked to the old ones, so changing the past is practically impossible.
It lets people agree on records without a central authority — the basis of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
artificial intelligence: Computer programs that do things that usually need human intelligence — recognising pictures, translating, answering questions — by learning patterns from lots of examples.
It's changing work, medicine and everyday tools — which is why people debate how to use it responsibly.
greenhouse effect: Some gases in the air let sunlight in but keep part of the heat from escaping — like the glass of a greenhouse.
A little of it keeps Earth warm enough to live on; too much (from burning fossil fuels) causes global warming.
volcano: An opening in the Earth's crust where hot melted rock (magma) from deep inside comes up as lava, ash and gas.
Eruptions can be dangerous, but volcanoes also create new land and very fertile soil.
earthquake: The ground shakes when huge plates of the Earth's crust suddenly slip past each other and release built-up tension.
Understanding them helps build safer houses and warn people in time.

subst.egg: No eggs? Per egg, mash half a ripe banana or use 3 tbsp applesauce — or just add a splash more milk and ½ tsp extra baking powder. They'll be a bit flatter, but still good.
subst.milk: No milk? Use the same amount of water or any plant milk (oat milk works great). With water they're just a little less rich.
subst.butter: No butter? Use the same amount of a neutral oil (sunflower or rapeseed) — works just as well.
subst.baking powder: No baking powder? Use ½ tsp baking soda plus 1 tbsp lemon juice or vinegar — or beat the egg white stiff and fold it in.
subst.sugar: Just leave it out, or use a little honey or maple syrup instead. For savoury versions you don't need any.
subst.flour: No flour? Blend oats into a fine powder and use about the same amount.

special.back hurts: Ugh, back pain is no fun. Gentle movement and warmth usually help more than lying still. If it lasts or gets worse, see a doctor.
special.stomach hurts: Oh no. Something light like tea and plain food may help. If it's severe or doesn't go away, please see a doctor.
special.chest hurts: Chest pain can be serious. If it's strong, spreads to your arm, jaw or back, or you're short of breath, call emergency services now (112 in Europe, 911 in the US).

f.a: That's common when you're just starting — usually it's too much too soon. Go a bit easier and shorter for a while, warm up properly, and check your technique and gear. If it hurts sharply, swells, or doesn't get better after a few days of rest, see a doctor or physio.

f.q: (?:so )?should i (?:stop|take a break|rest|keep going|keep running|continue|push through)(?: running| for a while)?
f.a: Not necessarily stop — take two or three days off, then go shorter and slower and see how it feels. If it hurts during the run, stop and get it checked. Pain is a signal, not something to push through.

f.a: If you can, go to a running shop — many let you try shoes and watch how you run. Comfort comes first: a thumb's width of room at the toes, nothing that pinches, and enough cushioning for road running. Replace them after roughly 600–800 km.

f.a:
A few things that help:

• Don't take the bait — answer lightly (“I like it this way”) and change the subject
• Give them something to do: cook together, go for a walk
• If it really hurts, say it once, calmly: “I know you mean well, but that upsets me.”
• Remember it's often their clumsy way of caring

And plan one nice thing together, so the visit isn't only about the criticism.

f.a:
Was oft hilft:

• Nicht anspringen – locker antworten („Mir gefällt's so“) und das Thema wechseln
• Gebt euch was zu tun: zusammen kochen, spazieren gehen
• Wenn es wirklich wehtut, einmal ruhig sagen: „Ich weiß, du meinst es gut, aber das verletzt mich.“
• Oft ist es ihre ungeschickte Art, sich zu kümmern

Und plant etwas Schönes zusammen, damit der Besuch nicht nur aus Kritik besteht.

phone: That's so normal — part of you is hoping for a message. It can help to mute the chat or put the phone in another room for a few hours.
sleep: Heartbreak does that — your mind keeps replaying everything. Writing down what's going round in your head before bed helps some people switch off.
advice:
For now, go easy on yourself:

• Let yourself feel it — being sad after a long relationship is normal
• Keep a small routine: eat, sleep, move a little
• Talk to people you trust
• Take a break from {z} social media

It gets lighter, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

fun_fact_basic: I don't have a special fun fact about {x} — but here are the basics: {y}

flight.japan: about 13–14 hours nonstop from Frankfurt or Munich to Tokyo — a bit longer than before 2022, because flights avoid Russian airspace.
flight.usa: about 8–9 hours to New York; the West Coast (Los Angeles, San Francisco) is about 11–12 hours.
flight.spain: about 2–2.5 hours to Barcelona or Madrid.
flight.italy: about 1.5–2 hours to Rome or Milan.
flight.egypt: about 4–5 hours to Cairo or Hurghada.
flight.mexico: about 11–12 hours to Mexico City or Cancún.
flight.brazil: about 11.5–12.5 hours to Rio or São Paulo.
flight.south africa: about 10.5–12 hours to Johannesburg or Cape Town.
flight.australia: there's no nonstop flight — with one stop (for example in Singapore, Dubai or Doha) it takes about 21–24 hours.
flight.indonesia: there's no nonstop flight to Bali — with one stop it takes about 16–18 hours.

flight_unknown: I don't have a reliable flight time for {x}, sorry — a flight search site will show the exact options.

currency.japan: the Japanese yen (¥). Japan still uses a lot of cash, so it's worth carrying some.

food.japan: Food to try in Japan: ramen, sushi and sashimi, tempura, okonomiyaki in Osaka, yakitori, gyoza, and onigiri from any convenience store — they're surprisingly good.
food.italy: Food to try in Italy: pasta the local way (carbonara in Rome, pesto in Genoa), real Neapolitan pizza, risotto in the north, and gelato every day.
food.spain: Food to try in Spain: tapas like patatas bravas and croquetas, paella in Valencia, jamón ibérico, and churros with chocolate.
food.france: Food to try in France: croissants from a boulangerie, crêpes, a proper cheese plate, steak frites, and whatever the bistro's dish of the day is.
food.greece: Food to try in Greece: souvlaki and gyros, moussaka, Greek salad with real feta, fresh seafood by the sea, and baklava.
food.thailand: Food to try in Thailand: pad thai, green curry, som tam (papaya salad), tom yum soup, and mango sticky rice — street food is often the best.
food.mexico: Food to try in Mexico: tacos al pastor, mole, tamales, fresh guacamole, and churros.
food.india: Food to try in India: biryani, butter chicken, dosa in the south, chaat from street stalls, and fresh naan.
food.portugal: Food to try in Portugal: pastéis de nata, grilled sardines, bacalhau, and a bifana sandwich.

sights.spain: Die Klassiker in Spanien: die Sagrada Família in Barcelona, der Prado in Madrid, die Alhambra in Granada, Sevilla und die Strände der Balearen.
sights.france: Die Klassiker in Frankreich: Paris mit Eiffelturm und Louvre, die Schlösser an der Loire, der Mont-Saint-Michel, die Provence und die Côte d'Azur.
sights.greece: Die Klassiker in Griechenland: die Akropolis in Athen, Santorini, die Klöster von Meteora, Delphi und Kreta.
sights.usa: Die Klassiker in den USA: New York, der Grand Canyon, San Francisco mit der Golden Gate Bridge, Yellowstone und Washington, D.C.
sights.portugal: Die Klassiker in Portugal: Lissabon mit Alfama und Belém, Porto am Douro, Sintra und die Algarve-Küste.

start_ask: Learning to code — great idea! Do you know which language yet? Python is a popular first one.
Oh, nice! Coding is a really useful skill. Any idea which language you want to start with?
start_lang: {x} — good choice! {y} Do you have something in mind you'd like to build?

lang.python: It's readable, forgiving for beginners, and you can do a lot with it quickly — scripts, data, websites, even little games.
lang.javascript: It runs in every browser, so you can see results on a web page right away.
lang.java: It's a bit more verbose, but very structured — and it's everywhere, from Android to big companies.
lang.c++: It's powerful and fast, but not the gentlest start — expect to fight the compiler a bit.
lang.c#: It's great for games with Unity and for Windows apps, and quite beginner-friendly.
lang.rust: It's loved for safety and speed, but it's a steep first language.
lang.go: It's simple, fast and popular for servers and tools.
lang.swift: It's the language for iPhone and Mac apps — nice if you want to build an app.
lang.kotlin: It's the modern choice for Android apps.
lang.html: Strictly it's not a programming language, but HTML and CSS are a great way to start — you build a web page on day one. JavaScript is the natural next step.
lang.ruby: It's friendly and readable, and known for the web framework Rails.
lang.php: It still powers a big part of the web, WordPress included.

hard: The start is easier than most people think — the first programs are just a few lines. The hard part is staying with it when something doesn't work, and that's normal for everyone. A little every day beats one long weekend.
Honestly? Not at the beginning. It gets tricky in places, but everyone gets stuck on bugs — even professionals. Patience matters more than talent.
how_long: For the basics — variables, loops, functions — a few weeks at 30 to 60 minutes a day. Building small projects on your own takes a few months. Getting job-ready is usually closer to a year of steady practice.
It depends on your goal: simple scripts after a few weeks, your own small projects after a few months, and job-level skills usually after about a year of regular practice.
where_start: Pick one free course and stick with it — for {x}, the official tutorial, freeCodeCamp or Harvard's free CS50 course are good. Then build something tiny you actually care about, like a to-do list or a quiz. Projects teach more than videos.

Start small: install {x}, follow one beginner course from start to finish (freeCodeCamp and CS50 are free), and code a little every day. After the basics, build a small project — that's where it clicks.
build: With {x} you could start with a number-guessing game, a to-do list, a little quiz, or a script that renames your files. Later: a website, a chatbot, or something with data you care about.

concept_offer: Let's untangle it together — want me to explain {X} in simple words?

simple.hypothesis testing: You start with a boring default assumption (the null hypothesis), e.g. “this coin is fair”. Then you collect data and ask: if the default were true, how likely is a result this extreme? That probability is the p-value. If it's very small (usually below 0.05), you reject the default — the data speak against it. If not, you keep it (which doesn't prove it's true).
simple.p-value: The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the default assumption (the null hypothesis) were true. Small p (like 0.01) = the data would be surprising under the default, so you doubt the default.
simple.standard deviation: Standard deviation says how spread out values are around the average. Small = most values close to the average; large = values scattered widely.
simple.derivative: A derivative measures how fast something changes — the slope of a curve at one point. Speed is the derivative of position over time.
simple.integral: An integral adds up infinitely many tiny pieces — for example the area under a curve, or the total distance from a changing speed.
simple.photosynthesis: Plants use sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar (their food) and release oxygen as a by-product.
simple.inflation: Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same money buys less. With 2 % inflation, something costing 100 € costs about 102 € a year later.
simple.compound interest: Compound interest is interest on interest: you earn interest not just on what you put in, but also on the interest you've already earned — so growth speeds up over time.
simple.supply and demand: When something is scarce and many want it, the price goes up; when there's plenty and few want it, the price goes down. The price settles where supply meets demand.
simple.regression: Regression draws the best-fitting line (or curve) through data points, so you can see how one thing changes with another and make predictions.
simple.correlation: Correlation measures how strongly two things move together, from -1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to +1 (in step). It doesn't prove that one causes the other.
simple.confidence interval: A confidence interval is a range that likely contains the true value. A 95 % interval means: if you repeated the study many times, about 95 % of those intervals would contain the true value.

cold_tips:
What helps most right now:

• Lots of warm drinks — tea with honey and lemon soothes the throat.
• Sleep early tonight; rest is the best medicine.
• Gargle with salt water, and suck throat lozenges.
• For tomorrow: keep water nearby while presenting and speak a bit slower to spare your voice.

heat_temp: 35 degrees — that's proper heat! Drink plenty and stay in the shade during the hottest hours.
heat_sleep: That's the worst — hot nights are exhausting.
heat_tips:
A few tricks:

• Keep windows and blinds shut during the day, open everything at night.
• A damp sheet or a cool shower before bed helps.
• Put a bowl of ice in front of a fan.
• A hot-water bottle filled with cold water in bed works wonders.
• Light cotton bedding, and drink enough during the day.
game_start: Oh nice — Elden Ring is famous for being tough but so rewarding. How are you finding it so far?
game_hard: It's hard for everyone at the start — that's part of the game's reputation. Every death teaches you something.
game_boss:
The first boss stops so many players! Here's what helps:

• Explore first and level up a bit — there's no shame in coming back stronger.
• Learn the attack patterns and roll *into* attacks, not away.
• Don't get greedy: one or two hits, then back off.
• Use Spirit Ash summons if you have them.
• And there's no rule that says you have to fight it now — the world is open.
game_tips: General tips: explore before fighting bosses, upgrade your weapon, use Spirit Ashes, and take breaks when you're frustrated — fresh eyes win fights. 😄
game_keep: That's the spirit! You'll get it — and the moment you beat it feels incredible. 🎮

ld_start: Das braucht viel Liebe und Geduld. Wie lange führt ihr schon eine Fernbeziehung?
ld_freq: Alle zwei Monate – da wird bestimmt viel heruntergezählt. Das Wiedersehen ist sicher schön, das Abschiednehmen umso härter.
ld_hard: Natürlich – jemanden zu vermissen, den man liebt, ist schwer, egal wie stark die Beziehung ist. Du darfst das hart finden.
ld_tips:
Was vielen Paaren hilft:

• Immer den nächsten Besuch schon gebucht haben – etwas zum Runterzählen.
• Regelmäßig telefonieren, aber auch „gemeinsam“ Dinge tun: zur gleichen Zeit einen Film schauen, dasselbe Rezept kochen.
• Kleine Überraschungen: ein Brief, ein Päckchen, eine Sprachnachricht.
• Ehrlich über schwere Tage reden, nicht nur über schöne.
• Eine gemeinsame Vorstellung davon, wann die Entfernung endet, macht viel aus.
tax_start: Ach, die Steuererklärung – niemandes Lieblingsaufgabe. Hast du schon mal eine gemacht, oder ist es die erste?
tax_putoff: Da bist du echt nicht allein. Meistens dauert es weniger lang, als das schlechte Gefühl vermuten lässt.
tax_where: Ganz normal. Mach den ersten Schritt winzig: diese Woche nur die Unterlagen in einen Ordner sammeln – sonst nichts. Soll ich dir noch Tipps für die Erklärung selbst geben?
tax_tips:
Was es leichter macht:

• Erst alles sammeln: Lohnsteuerbescheinigung, Belege für Werbungskosten, Versicherungen, Spenden.
• ELSTER oder eine Steuer-Software nutzen – die führen Schritt für Schritt durch.
• Zwei Stunden fest im Kalender blocken statt „irgendwann“.
• Mit dem Einfachen anfangen; der Rest wirkt dann kleiner.
• Wenn es kompliziert wird, lohnt sich ein Lohnsteuerhilfeverein oder eine Steuerberatung.
tax_weekend: Guter Plan – trag es dir wie einen Termin in den Kalender. Und gönn dir danach was! 🙌
guests_start: Wie schön, ein Essen mit Freunden! Wie viele kommen denn?
guests_count: {X} Leute – ein richtiges Essen! Gibt es was zu beachten, vegetarisch oder Allergien?
guests_veg: Gut zu wissen. Am einfachsten ist ein Hauptgericht, das alle essen können – dann bekommt der Gast mit vegetarischer Ernährung keine traurige Beilage. Soll ich Ideen geben?
guests_menu:
Für eine Runde mit Vegetarier:

• Ein großes Gemüse-Kichererbsen-Curry mit Reis und Naan
• Chili sin Carne mit vielen Toppings
• Ofengemüse-Lasagne
• Ein Risotto mit Pilzen

Alles lässt sich gut vorbereiten und für {X} Leute hochrechnen.
cold_throat: Klingt nach einer beginnenden Erkältung – gute Besserung! Ruhe, warme Getränke und viel Wasser helfen am meisten.
cold_tips:
Was jetzt am meisten hilft:

• Viel Warmes trinken – Tee mit Honig und Zitrone tut dem Hals gut.
• Heute früh schlafen; Ruhe ist die beste Medizin.
• Mit Salzwasser gurgeln, Halspastillen lutschen.
• Für morgen: Wasser bereitstellen und etwas langsamer sprechen, um die Stimme zu schonen.
• Bei Fieber oder wenn es deutlich schlimmer wird: Apotheke oder Arzt fragen.
heat_temp: 35 Grad – das ist richtig heiß! Viel trinken und in der Mittagshitze im Schatten bleiben.
heat_sleep: Das ist das Schlimmste – heiße Nächte sind zermürbend.
heat_tips:
Ein paar Tricks:

• Tagsüber Fenster und Rollläden zu, nachts alles auf.
• Ein feuchtes Laken oder eine kühle Dusche vor dem Schlafen.
• Eine Schüssel Eis vor den Ventilator stellen.
• Eine Wärmflasche mit kaltem Wasser ins Bett – wirkt Wunder.
• Leichte Baumwollbettwäsche und tagsüber genug trinken.
wl_start: Ein gutes Ziel! Machst du schon Sport, oder fängst du gerade an?
wl_gym: Zweimal die Woche ist eine super Basis! Krafttraining hilft besonders, weil Muskeln den Stoffwechsel oben halten.
wl_food: Beim Abnehmen zählt das Essen am meisten. Einfache Regeln, die funktionieren: viel Gemüse und Eiweiß (macht satt), weniger süße Getränke und Snacks, kleinere Portionen vom Kalorienreichen – und keine Crash-Diäten; kleine Änderungen hältst du viel länger durch.
wl_speed: Etwa ein halbes Kilo pro Woche ist realistisch und gesund – 5 Kilo dauern also ungefähr 10–12 Wochen. Schneller heißt meist Wasser und Muskeln, und das kommt schnell zurück.

kidtest_start: Oh, a big day for him! How's he feeling about it?
kidtest_anx: Poor thing — first big tests feel huge at that age. The good news: a bit of nervousness actually helps you focus.
kidtest_stomach: That's very typical — nerves often show up as a tummy ache in kids. A calm evening, a light dinner and an early night help more than any extra studying now.
kidtest_say:
A few things that usually help:

• “It's okay to be nervous — it means you care.”
• “I'm proud of you for practising, whatever the result.”
• “If you get stuck, skip it and come back later.”
• Practise one slow breath together: in for four, out for six.
• And a little note in his pencil case for tomorrow can work wonders. 💛
move_start: Exciting — and a lot of work! Is it a big move or just across town?
move_stuff: Moving is the perfect moment to declutter — everything you don't pack, you don't have to carry.
move_where: Start where it hurts least: one box of things you won't need before the move — books, decorations, the guest room. Once the first boxes are packed, it gets easier. Want a few more packing tips?
puppy_scratch: Ouch — those little puppy teeth are like needles! Clean the scratches and hang in there; there are a few tricks that really help.
move_tips:
A few packing tips:

• Start with the rooms and things you use least (books, guest room, decorations).
• Declutter as you go: keep, donate, bin.
• Label every box with room + contents, and number them.
• Pack a “first night” box: chargers, toiletries, bedding, kettle, snacks.
• Heavy things in small boxes, light things in big ones.
• Take photos of cable setups before you unplug them.
move_room: Exactly — one room at a time keeps it manageable. Start with the one you use least. 📦
wed_small: A small wedding is lovely — more time with each guest and much less stress.
wed_guests: Around 40 guests is a great size — big enough to feel like a party, small enough to stay personal.
wed_steps:
A good order to start in:

• Agree on a rough budget together.
• Pick a date (or a season) and the size — you've got that already.
• Book the venue first — popular ones go 12+ months ahead.
• Then the big helpers: photographer, caterer, and an officiant or registry office.
• Send save-the-dates once date and venue are fixed.

Everything else (dress, flowers, music) can follow later.
credit_start: Ugh, that's so frustrating — and unfair. Has it happened before?
credit_again: Again? Then it's not an accident anymore. You have every right to be annoyed.
credit_boss: It's worth raising — but calmly and with facts. What often works: first talk to the colleague directly (“I noticed my analysis was presented as yours — let's make sure credit is clear”). If it continues, go to your boss with concrete examples. And from now on, share your work in writing, e.g. by email with your boss in CC, so it's visible who did what.
credit_first: Good plan — talking to her first is fair and often enough. Keep it calm and factual. Good luck! 💪
puppy_start: Ah, the land-shark phase! 🦈 How old is she?
puppy_age: 3 months — that's peak teething time, so the biting is completely normal. The good news: it usually gets much better by 5–6 months.
puppy_tips:
What works for most puppies:

• When she bites, say a short “ouch!” and stop playing for a moment — fun ends when teeth touch skin.
• Immediately offer a chew toy instead and praise her when she takes it.
• Frozen carrots or a wet, frozen cloth soothe teething gums.
• Avoid wild hand-games — use toys, not hands.
• Make sure she gets enough sleep: overtired puppies bite more (they need 16–18 hours!).
cook_pasta: Pasta is a great start — if you can make good pasta, you already know the basics of timing and seasoning.
cook_first:
Great next steps:

• A proper tomato sauce from scratch (onion, garlic, tinned tomatoes) — the base of so many dishes.
• Eggs three ways: scrambled, fried, omelette.
• A simple stir-fry with rice — teaches chopping and high heat.
• Roast vegetables in the oven with olive oil and salt.
• A basic soup.

One new dish a week and you'll have a real repertoire in two months.
bike_never: No problem — a flat is one of the easiest repairs to learn.
bike_hard:
Not really — it takes about 20 minutes the first time. You need tyre levers, a patch kit (or a new inner tube) and a pump:

• Take the wheel off and lever the tyre off on one side.
• Pull out the tube, pump it up a bit and find the hole (listen, or dip it in water).
• Roughen the spot, glue, wait a minute, press the patch on.
• Check the tyre for the thorn or glass that caused it!
• Put everything back and pump up.

There are great step-by-step videos if you want to watch it once.
bike_go: You've got this! And once you've done it once, you'll never need a bike shop for a flat again. 🚲
jazz_albums:
Classic jazz albums people love:

• Miles Davis – “Kind of Blue”
• John Coltrane – “A Love Supreme”
• Dave Brubeck Quartet – “Time Out”
• Bill Evans Trio – “Waltz for Debby”
• Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong – “Ella and Louis”

“Kind of Blue” is the perfect place to start.

kidtest_start: Oh, ein großer Tag für ihn! Wie geht's ihm damit?
kidtest_anx: Der Arme – die ersten großen Arbeiten fühlen sich in dem Alter riesig an. Das Gute: Ein bisschen Aufregung hilft sogar beim Konzentrieren.
kidtest_stomach: Das ist ganz typisch – Aufregung schlägt Kindern oft auf den Bauch. Ein ruhiger Abend, ein leichtes Abendessen und früh schlafen helfen jetzt mehr als noch mehr Lernen.
kidtest_say:
Was meistens hilft:

• „Aufgeregt zu sein ist okay – das zeigt, dass es dir wichtig ist.“
• „Ich bin stolz auf dich, dass du geübt hast, egal wie es ausgeht.“
• „Wenn du hängst, überspring die Aufgabe und komm später zurück.“
• Gemeinsam einmal langsam atmen: vier Sekunden ein, sechs aus.
• Und ein kleiner Zettel im Mäppchen für morgen wirkt Wunder. 💛
move_start: Spannend – und viel Arbeit! Ist es ein großer Umzug oder nur innerhalb der Stadt?
move_stuff: Ein Umzug ist die perfekte Gelegenheit zum Ausmisten – alles, was du nicht packst, musst du auch nicht tragen.
move_where: Fang da an, wo es am wenigsten wehtut: ein Karton mit Sachen, die du vor dem Umzug nicht mehr brauchst – Bücher, Deko, Gästezimmer. Wenn die ersten Kartons stehen, wird es leichter. Soll ich dir noch ein paar Pack-Tipps geben?
move_tips:
Ein paar Pack-Tipps:

• Mit den Räumen und Sachen anfangen, die du am wenigsten brauchst (Bücher, Gästezimmer, Deko).
• Beim Packen gleich ausmisten: behalten, spenden, weg.
• Jeden Karton mit Raum und Inhalt beschriften und nummerieren.
• Eine „Erste-Nacht-Kiste“ packen: Ladekabel, Kulturbeutel, Bettzeug, Wasserkocher, Snacks.
• Schweres in kleine Kartons, Leichtes in große.
• Kabel fotografieren, bevor du sie absteckst.
move_room: Genau – ein Zimmer nach dem anderen, dann bleibt es überschaubar. Fang mit dem an, das du am wenigsten nutzt. 📦
wed_small: Eine kleine Hochzeit ist wunderschön – mehr Zeit für jeden Gast und viel weniger Stress.
wed_guests: Um die 40 Gäste ist eine tolle Größe – groß genug für ein Fest, klein genug, um persönlich zu bleiben.
wed_steps:
Eine gute Reihenfolge für den Start:

• Gemeinsam ein grobes Budget festlegen.
• Datum (oder Jahreszeit) und Größe wählen – die Größe habt ihr schon.
• Zuerst die Location buchen – beliebte sind 12 Monate und mehr im Voraus weg.
• Dann Standesamt, Fotograf und Catering.
• „Save the Date“ verschicken, sobald Datum und Ort feststehen.

Alles andere (Kleid, Blumen, Musik) kann später kommen.
credit_start: Boah, das ist echt frustrierend – und unfair. Ist das schon öfter passiert?
credit_again: Schon wieder? Dann ist das kein Versehen mehr. Du hast jedes Recht, sauer zu sein.
credit_boss: Ansprechen lohnt sich – aber ruhig und mit Fakten. Was oft funktioniert: zuerst direkt mit dem Kollegen reden („Mir ist aufgefallen, dass meine Auswertung als deine präsentiert wurde – lass uns klarstellen, wer was gemacht hat“). Wenn es weitergeht, mit konkreten Beispielen zum Chef. Und ab jetzt Arbeitsergebnisse schriftlich teilen, zum Beispiel per Mail mit dem Chef in CC.
puppy_start: Ah, die Haifisch-Phase! 🦈 Wie alt ist sie denn?
puppy_age: 3 Monate – genau die Zeit des Zahnwechsels, das Beißen ist völlig normal. Die gute Nachricht: Mit 5–6 Monaten wird es meist deutlich besser.
puppy_tips:
Was bei den meisten Welpen hilft:

• Wenn sie zubeißt, kurz „Aua!“ sagen und das Spiel kurz unterbrechen – der Spaß endet, wenn Zähne Haut berühren.
• Sofort ein Kauspielzeug anbieten und loben, wenn sie es nimmt.
• Gefrorene Karotten oder ein nasses, eingefrorenes Tuch beruhigen das Zahnfleisch.
• Keine wilden Handspiele – Spielzeug statt Hände.
• Genug Schlaf: Übermüdete Welpen beißen mehr (sie brauchen 16–18 Stunden!).
bike_never: Kein Problem – ein Platten ist eine der einfachsten Reparaturen überhaupt.
bike_hard:
Eigentlich nicht – beim ersten Mal dauert es etwa 20 Minuten. Du brauchst Reifenheber, Flickzeug (oder einen neuen Schlauch) und eine Pumpe:

• Rad ausbauen und den Mantel auf einer Seite abhebeln.
• Schlauch rausnehmen, etwas aufpumpen und das Loch suchen (hören oder ins Wasser halten).
• Stelle anrauen, Kleber drauf, kurz warten, Flicken andrücken.
• Den Mantel nach dem Dorn oder der Scherbe absuchen!
• Alles wieder einbauen und aufpumpen.
bike_go: Du schaffst das! Und wenn du es einmal gemacht hast, brauchst du für einen Platten nie wieder die Werkstatt. 🚲

date_start: Ooh, exciting! A first date — how did you meet?
date_nervous: Totally normal — being nervous just means you care. And they're probably just as nervous as you are.
date_coffee: Coffee is a great first date: relaxed, not too long, and easy to extend if it goes well. ☕
date_talk:
Easy, low-pressure topics:

• Travel — where they've been, where they'd love to go.
• What they do in their free time, and what they're excited about lately.
• Favourite food, films or series — and the “guilty pleasure” version.
• Funny small stories (worst holiday, weirdest job).

Ask open questions, really listen, and pick up on what lights them up. And it's fine to have a short pause — that's normal.
phone_start: Oh no, the classic! Is it still working at least?
phone_works: At least it still works. Put a cheap screen protector over the crack so it doesn't spread or cut your finger.
phone_worth: It depends on the phone. A screen repair usually costs 80–250 €, depending on the model. Rule of thumb: if the repair costs less than about a third of a new phone and the rest still works well, repairing is worth it. How old is it?
phone_age: At two years old it's usually worth repairing — the phone still has a few good years in it. Ask an independent repair shop for a quote; they're often cheaper than the manufacturer.
phone_quote: Good plan — and ask whether they use original or third-party parts; that affects price and quality.
parents_start: That's a big thing to think about. How are they doing at the moment?
parents_worry: Of course you do — that's love. Worrying from a distance is especially hard.
parents_distance: Three hours is far enough to make spontaneous visits hard. That's a real strain.
parents_tips:
A few things that help many families:

• A fixed weekly call — maybe a video call, so you see how they're doing.
• Know their doctors, medication and important contacts, and keep a list.
• Get to know a neighbour or friend nearby who could check in if needed.
• Plan visits regularly, and use them to look out for small changes.
• Talk early and openly about what they want if they need more help one day.
email_start: Oh no, inbox overload — that's exhausting. How many are we talking about?
email_count: 200 a day? No wonder there's no time for real work.
email_cant: That's the classic trap — email eats the day. Want a few tricks that really help?
email_tricks:
A few that really work:

• Check email at fixed times (e.g. 9, 12, 16) instead of constantly.
• Turn off notifications.
• The 2-minute rule: if it takes under 2 minutes, do it now — otherwise schedule it.
• Filters and folders for newsletters, CCs and automatic mails.
• Block 1–2 hours a day for real work, with email closed.
• Unsubscribe from everything you never read.
email_try: Great — start with the fixed email times; it's the one that makes the biggest difference. Good luck! 💪
balcony_start: Lovely idea! How much sun does the balcony get?
balcony_sun: Morning sun is actually great — many plants love it, and they don't get scorched in the afternoon.
balcony_easy:
Easy winners for a morning-sun balcony:

• Herbs: parsley, chives, mint, basil (basil likes a bit more sun)
• Salad leaves and rocket — fast and forgiving
• Strawberries in a hanging basket
• Cherry tomatoes (a sunny corner helps)
• Flowers: geraniums, petunias, nasturtiums (edible, too!)

Good soil, pots with drainage holes and regular watering are 90 % of the job.
balcony_beginner: Perfect — then start with 3–4 easy herbs and some salad. They grow quickly, so you see results fast and learn as you go. 🌱
swim_start: Honestly, lots of adults can't swim — you're far from alone.
swim_embarrassed: Please don't be! It takes courage to want to learn as an adult.
swim_late: It's never too late. Many pools offer adult beginner courses — usually small groups and very patient instructors. Most adults can swim a few lengths after 8–10 lessons.
swim_book: That's a great step! Look for an “adult beginners” course — you'll be in good company. 🏊
return_start: Annoying! Online shoe sizes are a lottery.
return_ship: In the EU you have a 14-day right of withdrawal for online purchases. The shop may make you pay the return shipping — but only if they told you so clearly before you bought. If they didn't, they have to cover it. Many shops pay it anyway, so check their returns page.
return_allowed: Only if they told you clearly before you bought — otherwise they have to cover it. Worth checking their terms!
babysit_start: That sounds fun! How old is she?
babysit_age: 6 is a lovely age — curious and full of energy.
babysit_ideas:
A few ideas for a 6-year-old:

• Build a blanket fort and read stories inside with a torch
• Bake simple cookies or decorate pancakes
• Drawing, crafts or a mini treasure hunt
• A board game like Memory or Uno
• A dance party to her favourite songs
babysit_animals:
Then animal ideas are perfect:

• Watch a nature documentary or an animal film together
• Make paper animal masks and play zoo
• Animal charades: act one out, the other guesses
• Draw her dream pet and invent its name and story
• If it's still light: a walk to look for birds, squirrels or ducks 🐿️

date_start: Oh, spannend! Ein erstes Date – wie habt ihr euch kennengelernt?
date_nervous: Ganz normal – Nervosität heißt nur, dass es dir wichtig ist. Und die andere Person ist wahrscheinlich genauso aufgeregt.
date_coffee: Kaffee ist ein super erstes Date: locker, nicht zu lang, und wenn es gut läuft, kann man es leicht verlängern. ☕
date_talk:
Lockere Themen, die fast immer funktionieren:

• Reisen – wo die Person schon war, wo sie gern hinwill.
• Was sie in ihrer Freizeit macht und worauf sie sich gerade freut.
• Lieblingsessen, Filme, Serien – auch die heimlichen Favoriten.
• Lustige kleine Geschichten (schlimmster Urlaub, seltsamster Job).

Offene Fragen stellen, wirklich zuhören und auf das eingehen, wobei die Augen leuchten. Kurze Pausen sind völlig normal.
phone_start: Oh nein, der Klassiker! Funktioniert es wenigstens noch?
phone_works: Immerhin geht es noch. Kleb eine günstige Schutzfolie drüber, damit der Sprung nicht weiterreißt und du dich nicht schneidest.
phone_worth: Kommt aufs Handy an. Ein neues Display kostet meist 80–250 €, je nach Modell. Faustregel: Wenn die Reparatur weniger als etwa ein Drittel eines neuen Handys kostet und der Rest noch gut läuft, lohnt sie sich. Wie alt ist es denn?
phone_age: Bei zwei Jahren lohnt sich die Reparatur meistens – da ist noch einiges drin. Frag bei einem freien Reparaturshop nach einem Angebot; die sind oft günstiger als der Hersteller.
parents_start: Das ist ein großes Thema. Wie geht es ihnen gerade?
parents_distance: Drei Stunden sind weit genug, dass spontane Besuche schwierig werden. Das ist echt belastend.
parents_tips:
Was vielen Familien hilft:

• Ein fester wöchentlicher Anruf – gern per Video, damit du siehst, wie es ihnen geht.
• Ärzte, Medikamente und wichtige Kontakte kennen und notieren.
• Jemanden in der Nähe kennen (Nachbarn, Freunde), der im Notfall vorbeischauen kann.
• Regelmäßige Besuche einplanen und dabei auf kleine Veränderungen achten.
• Früh und offen darüber reden, was sie sich wünschen, falls sie irgendwann mehr Hilfe brauchen.
email_start: Oh nein, Postfach-Flut – das ist echt zermürbend. Um wie viele geht es denn?
email_count: 200 am Tag? Kein Wunder, dass für echte Arbeit keine Zeit bleibt.
email_cant: Die klassische Falle – E-Mails fressen den Tag. Soll ich dir ein paar Tricks verraten, die wirklich helfen?
email_tricks:
Ein paar, die wirklich funktionieren:

• E-Mails zu festen Zeiten checken (z. B. 9, 12, 16 Uhr) statt ständig.
• Benachrichtigungen ausschalten.
• Zwei-Minuten-Regel: Was unter zwei Minuten dauert, sofort erledigen – sonst einplanen.
• Filter und Ordner für Newsletter, CC und automatische Mails.
• Täglich 1–2 Stunden für echte Arbeit blocken, mit geschlossenem Postfach.
• Alles abbestellen, was du nie liest.
email_try: Super – fang mit den festen E-Mail-Zeiten an, das bringt am meisten. Viel Erfolg! 💪
balcony_start: Schöne Idee! Wie viel Sonne bekommt der Balkon denn?
balcony_sun: Morgensonne ist sogar super – viele Pflanzen mögen das und verbrennen nicht in der Nachmittagshitze.
balcony_easy:
Leichte Kandidaten für einen Balkon mit Morgensonne:

• Kräuter: Petersilie, Schnittlauch, Minze, Basilikum (mag etwas mehr Sonne)
• Pflücksalat und Rucola – schnell und unkompliziert
• Erdbeeren in einer Hängeampel
• Cocktailtomaten (eine sonnige Ecke hilft)
• Blumen: Geranien, Petunien, Kapuzinerkresse (sogar essbar!)

Gute Erde, Töpfe mit Abzugsloch und regelmäßiges Gießen sind 90 % der Arbeit.
babysit_start: Das klingt schön! Wie alt ist sie denn?
babysit_age: 6 ist ein tolles Alter – neugierig und voller Energie.
babysit_ideas:
Ein paar Ideen für eine Sechsjährige:

• Eine Deckenhöhle bauen und darin mit Taschenlampe vorlesen
• Einfache Kekse backen oder Pfannkuchen verzieren
• Malen, Basteln oder eine kleine Schatzsuche
• Ein Spiel wie Memory oder Uno
• Eine Tanzparty zu ihren Lieblingsliedern
babysit_animals:
Dann sind Tier-Ideen perfekt:

• Zusammen eine Tierdoku oder einen Tierfilm schauen
• Tiermasken aus Papier basteln und Zoo spielen
• Tier-Pantomime: einer spielt vor, der andere rät
• Ihr Traumhaustier malen und Name und Geschichte erfinden
• Wenn es noch hell ist: ein Spaziergang, um Vögel, Eichhörnchen oder Enten zu entdecken 🐿️

lock_start: Oh no! Does a neighbour, friend or your landlord have a spare key? Otherwise a locksmith — ask for the price first.
bday_start: Oops — it happens to everyone. A call today and a small belated surprise usually make up for it.
wash_start: Oh no, the {x}! That's so annoying. Can it be fixed, or is it time for a new one?
smoke_start: That takes real willpower — good for you! How much do you smoke at the moment?
lock_inside: The classic: door shut, keys on the wrong side. Is there anyone nearby who might have a spare?
lock_late: At that hour a locksmith usually adds a night surcharge, so a spare key is worth trying first. Anyone you could call?
lock_smith: If nobody has a spare: yes. But ask for the total price on the phone before they come. At night 100–250 € is common, and dodgy services charge far more. A good locksmith can usually open a door that's just pulled shut without damaging the lock.
lock_spare: Perfect — that saves you a lot of money and hassle! Maybe leave a spare with them for good from now on. 🔑
hair_start: Oh no! A bad haircut really gets to you. What went wrong?
hair_short: Too short is the hardest kind, because there's nothing to fix — you can only wait it out.
hair_uneven: Uneven is annoying — but that's the good kind of bad haircut: a hairdresser can usually even it out in ten minutes. Many salons fix their own mistakes for free.
hair_event: Of course it had to happen right before a {x}! But a fresh cut always looks harsher on day one than a few days later.
hair_okay: Very likely, yes. A fresh cut always looks harsher on the first day — after a few days it settles. A bit of styling product helps, and if it's uneven, a quick fix at the salon sorts it out.
hair_grow: Honestly, not much: hair grows about a centimetre a month. But in a few days it won't look so ‘fresh’ any more, and a bit of styling product plus a nice outfit work wonders. Wear it confidently — short hair looks intentional when you own it.
bday_when: Only a day late — that's very fixable. A belated wish still shows you care.
bday_when_more: A few days late is still very fixable — a belated wish shows you care, and the sooner the better.
bday_awful: The guilt shows how much {who} means to you. But one forgotten birthday doesn't undo a relationship.
bday_fix:
A few ideas:

• Call {pron} today — don't just text. Own it: “I'm so sorry, I completely forgot.” No excuses.
• Plan a belated celebration: coffee, cake or dinner, your treat.
• A small, personal gift beats an expensive one — something that shows you know {pron}.
• Put important birthdays in your phone calendar, with a reminder a few days ahead.

Most people are much more forgiving than we fear, especially when the apology is honest.
bday_ok: Good plan — I'm sure {who} will appreciate it. Let me know how it goes! 🎂
tooth_start: Ouch, toothache is the worst. How long has it been hurting?
tooth_days: If it's been going on that long, it probably won't go away on its own — worth getting it checked soon.
tooth_cold: Pain with cold often points to an exposed tooth neck or a small cavity. A toothpaste for sensitive teeth can help for now, but a dentist should take a look.
tooth_bite: Pain when biting can mean a crack, a cavity or an inflamed root. It's worth getting it checked soon — chew on the other side until then.
tooth_today: If it's bearable, an appointment in the next day or two is usually fine. Go today or to an emergency dentist if your cheek swells, you get a fever, the pain throbs constantly or painkillers don't help.
tooth_wait: If it only hurts with cold and is bearable, waiting until then is usually okay; ibuprofen or paracetamol help in the meantime. But go to an emergency dentist straight away if your cheek swells, you get a fever, the pain throbs constantly or keeps you awake.
tooth_call: Good call. Tell them it's been hurting for a few days — many practices keep slots free for people in pain. Get well soon! 🦷
wash_leak: First turn off the water tap behind it and unplug it, then put towels down. Often it's just the filter, a hose or the door seal — the filter at the bottom front is the first thing to check.
wash_age_young: That's middle age for a {x} — they often last 10–15 years. So a repair can still be well worth it.
wash_age_old: That's a good age for a {x} already. A repair is only worth it if it's something small and cheap.
wash_decide: Rule of thumb: if the repair costs less than about half the price of a new machine, repair it. A technician's visit plus a small part (pump, hose, seal) is often 100–200 €; a decent new machine starts around 350–400 €. Ask for a quote first — if it's the drum bearings or the motor, a new one is usually the better deal.
wash_decide_old: At that age I'd only repair it if it's something small like a hose, the filter or a seal. If it's the motor, the bearings or the electronics, a new machine is usually the better deal — newer ones also use much less water and power.
smoke_count: That's a real habit — but at that level lots of people manage to quit, especially with a plan.
smoke_failed: That's completely normal — most ex-smokers needed several attempts. Every try teaches you more about your triggers.
smoke_help:
What helps most, according to the evidence:

• Pick a quit date in the next two weeks and tell people about it.
• Nicotine replacement (patches, gum, lozenges) roughly doubles your chances — ask at a pharmacy or your doctor.
• Know your triggers (coffee, stress, after meals, alcohol) and plan a replacement: a short walk, gum, a glass of water.
• Get rid of cigarettes, lighters and ashtrays before the day.
• Free quit lines and quit apps make a real difference.
• A craving peaks for a few minutes, then passes — ride it out.
smoke_date: Great step! Write it down and tell someone you trust. I'm rooting for you. 💪
thesis_start: Oh, the thesis procrastination spiral — very common. When's the deadline?
thesis_deadline: That's tight but doable — if you start properly this week.
thesis_youtube: Totally human — the brain picks the easy reward over the scary task. It's usually not laziness; the task just feels too big.
thesis_how:
Make it small and concrete:

• Tiny first step: “open the document and write three sentences”, not “write chapter 2”.
• Work in 25-minute blocks with 5-minute breaks (Pomodoro).
• Phone in another room, and YouTube blocked during work blocks (a site blocker helps).
• Plan backwards: what has to be done in each of the remaining weeks?
• Same place, same time every day — the routine does the work.
• Tell your supervisor or a friend your goal for the week.
thesis_try: Good luck! Start with just one small block today — the first ten minutes are the hardest part. 📚
room_start: Ugh, living with a messy roommate is draining. What bothers you most?
room_dishes: Dishes piling up are the number one flat-share argument — you're definitely not alone.
room_mess: Living in someone else's mess is exhausting — you're definitely not alone with that.
room_fight: Makes sense — you have to live together. The good news: one calm talk usually works better than months of silent frustration.
room_bring:
A few things that help:

• Pick a calm moment — not when you're annoyed or the sink is overflowing.
• Use “I” sentences: “I find it hard to cook when the sink is full” instead of “You're so messy”.
• Suggest a solution: a simple cleaning rota, or “dishes done the same day”.
• Ask what bothers them too — that keeps it fair.
• Start friendly: they may genuinely not notice.

lock_start: Oh nein! Hat ein Nachbar, Freund oder der Vermieter einen Ersatzschlüssel? Sonst Schlüsseldienst – vorher nach dem Preis fragen.
wash_start: So ein Pech! Ist es etwas, das sich reparieren lässt?
lock_inside: Der Klassiker: Tür zu, Schlüssel auf der falschen Seite. Wohnt jemand in der Nähe, der einen Ersatzschlüssel haben könnte?
lock_late: Um die Uhrzeit verlangen Schlüsseldienste meist einen Nachtzuschlag – ein Ersatzschlüssel lohnt sich also erst recht. Kannst du jemanden anrufen?
lock_smith: Wenn niemand einen Ersatzschlüssel hat: ja. Aber lass dir am Telefon vorher den Gesamtpreis nennen. Nachts sind 100–250 € üblich, unseriöse Dienste verlangen deutlich mehr. Eine nur zugezogene Tür kann ein guter Schlüsseldienst meist ohne Schaden öffnen.
lock_spare: Perfekt – das spart dir viel Geld und Ärger! Vielleicht lässt du ab jetzt dauerhaft einen Ersatzschlüssel dort. 🔑
hair_start: Oh nein! Ein misslungener Haarschnitt nervt richtig. Was ist schiefgelaufen?
hair_short: Zu kurz ist am schlimmsten, weil man nichts mehr korrigieren kann – nur abwarten.
hair_uneven: Schief ist ärgerlich – aber die gute Sorte misslungener Haarschnitt: Das kann ein Friseur meist in zehn Minuten ausgleichen. Viele Salons korrigieren eigene Fehler kostenlos.
hair_event: Natürlich genau vor {x}! Aber ein frischer Schnitt wirkt am ersten Tag immer härter als ein paar Tage später.
hair_grow: Ehrlich gesagt nicht viel: Haare wachsen etwa einen Zentimeter im Monat. Aber nach ein paar Tagen wirkt es nicht mehr so „frisch“, und mit etwas Stylingprodukt und einem schönen Outfit fällt es kaum auf. Trag es selbstbewusst – dann wirkt kurz gewollt.
bday_start: Oh je – das passiert wirklich jedem mal. Wann war er denn?
bday_when: Nur einen Tag zu spät – das lässt sich gut retten. Ein nachträglicher Glückwunsch zeigt trotzdem, dass {subject} dir wichtig ist.
bday_when_more: Ein paar Tage zu spät lässt sich immer noch gut retten – je schneller du dich meldest, desto besser.
bday_awful: Das schlechte Gewissen zeigt, wie wichtig {subject} dir ist. Aber ein vergessener Geburtstag macht keine Beziehung kaputt.
bday_fix:
Ein paar Ideen:

• Ruf {pron} heute an – nicht nur schreiben. Steh dazu: „Es tut mir so leid, ich hab's total vergessen.“ Keine Ausreden.
• Plan eine nachträgliche Feier: Kaffee, Kuchen oder Essen, du lädst ein.
• Ein kleines, persönliches Geschenk wirkt mehr als ein teures.
• Trag wichtige Geburtstage mit Erinnerung ein paar Tage vorher in den Handykalender ein.

Die meisten verzeihen viel schneller, als man befürchtet – vor allem bei einer ehrlichen Entschuldigung.
bday_ok: Gute Idee – da wird {subject} sich bestimmt freuen. Erzähl mir gern, wie es gelaufen ist! 🎂
tooth_start: Autsch, Zahnschmerzen sind das Schlimmste. Seit wann tut es denn weh?
tooth_days: Wenn es schon so lange anhält, geht es wahrscheinlich nicht von allein weg – lass es bald anschauen.
tooth_cold: Schmerzen bei Kälte deuten oft auf einen freiliegenden Zahnhals oder ein kleines Loch hin. Eine Zahnpasta für empfindliche Zähne hilft vorübergehend, aber ein Zahnarzt sollte draufschauen.
tooth_bite: Schmerzen beim Kauen können auf einen Riss, ein Loch oder eine entzündete Wurzel hindeuten. Lass es bald anschauen – bis dahin am besten auf der anderen Seite kauen.
tooth_today: Wenn es auszuhalten ist, reicht meist ein Termin in den nächsten ein, zwei Tagen. Heute oder zum Notdienst solltest du, wenn die Wange anschwillt, du Fieber bekommst, es ständig pocht oder Schmerzmittel nicht helfen.
tooth_wait: Wenn es nur bei Kälte wehtut und auszuhalten ist, kannst du meist bis dahin warten; Ibuprofen oder Paracetamol helfen in der Zwischenzeit. Geh aber sofort zum zahnärztlichen Notdienst, wenn die Wange anschwillt, du Fieber bekommst, es ständig pocht oder dich nicht schlafen lässt.
tooth_call: Gute Entscheidung. Sag, dass es seit ein paar Tagen wehtut – viele Praxen halten Termine für Schmerzpatienten frei. Gute Besserung! 🦷
wash_leak: Dreh zuerst den Wasserhahn dahinter zu und zieh den Stecker, dann Handtücher drunter. Oft ist es nur das Flusensieb, ein Schlauch oder die Türdichtung – das Sieb unten vorne zuerst prüfen.
wash_age_young: Das ist für {x} mittleres Alter – viele halten 10 bis 15 Jahre. Eine Reparatur kann sich also durchaus lohnen.
wash_age_old: Das ist schon ein gutes Alter für {x}. Eine Reparatur lohnt sich nur, wenn es etwas Kleines und Günstiges ist.
wash_decide: Faustregel: Wenn die Reparatur weniger als etwa die Hälfte einer neuen Maschine kostet, reparieren. Techniker plus kleines Teil (Pumpe, Schlauch, Dichtung) kosten oft 100–200 €, eine ordentliche neue Maschine gibt es ab etwa 350–400 €. Lass dir vorher einen Kostenvoranschlag geben – sind es die Trommellager oder der Motor, ist eine neue meist die bessere Wahl.
wash_decide_old: In dem Alter würde ich nur reparieren, wenn es etwas Kleines ist, etwa Schlauch, Sieb oder Dichtung. Sind es Motor, Lager oder Elektronik, ist eine neue meist die bessere Wahl – neue Maschinen brauchen auch deutlich weniger Wasser und Strom.
smoke_start: Das ist eine richtig gute Entscheidung! Wie viel rauchst du denn im Moment?
smoke_count: Das ist schon eine Gewohnheit – aber in dem Bereich schaffen es viele, vor allem mit einem Plan.
smoke_failed: Das ist völlig normal – die meisten Ex-Raucher haben mehrere Anläufe gebraucht. Jeder Versuch zeigt dir mehr über deine Auslöser.
smoke_help:
Was laut Studien am meisten hilft:

• Ein festes Rauchstopp-Datum in den nächsten zwei Wochen – und anderen davon erzählen.
• Nikotinersatz (Pflaster, Kaugummi, Lutschtabletten) verdoppelt etwa die Chancen – frag in der Apotheke oder beim Hausarzt.
• Deine Auslöser kennen (Kaffee, Stress, nach dem Essen, Alkohol) und einen Ersatz planen: kurz rausgehen, Kaugummi, ein Glas Wasser.
• Zigaretten, Feuerzeuge und Aschenbecher vorher wegwerfen.
• Kostenlose Beratung, etwa das Rauchfrei-Telefon (0800 8 31 31 31), und Rauchstopp-Apps helfen spürbar.
• Ein Rauchverlangen ist nach ein paar Minuten vorbei – aushalten lohnt sich.
smoke_date: Super Schritt! Schreib es dir auf und erzähl es jemandem, dem du vertraust. Ich drück dir die Daumen. 💪
